an.chain: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout").
senses: The prefix conveys contact or attachment — fastening one thing onto another.
The prefix conveys approach and arrival — motion directed toward a destination.
The prefix is inchoative: it marks the beginning of an action rather than its whole course.
The prefix marks a partial action — doing something a little, not all the way.
The prefix directs the action at an addressee — speaking, presenting, or announcing to someone.
The prefix marks an action or state continuing over a stretch of time.
The prefix marks bringing something into being by mixing or preparing it — the base action produces the thing itself.
The prefix marks accumulation or acquisition — building up a holding until it is full or obtained.
The prefix directs the action against a resistance, usually alongside a ~gegen~ complement.

aneinander.chain: Transparently ~an~ ("at, on, against") + ~einander~ ("one another"), the reciprocal pronoun from MHG ~ein ander~. The compound is reciprocal rather than deictic: it says that the participants act on each other, as in ~aneinandergeraten~ ("to come to blows") or ~aneinanderreihen~ ("to string together"). See the entries for ~an~ and for the parallel formation ~durcheinander~.
senses: The sense of ~aneinander-~ here is: one against or onto another — reciprocal contact.
The sense of ~aneinander-~ here is: joined end to end, in a row.
The sense of ~aneinander-~ here is: into conflict with one another.

anheim.chain: A frozen adverbial phrase, ~an~ + ~heim~, in which ~heim~ is the old directional accusative "homeward" rather than the locative ~heime~ ("at home"). Early New High German added ~an-~ to make the directional sense explicit once accusative and dative had fallen together in form. The phrase no longer exists as a free adverb and survives only in ~anheimfallen~ ("to pass into someone's possession") and ~anheimstellen~ ("to leave to someone's discretion"), both of elevated register; ~heim~ is cognate with English ~home~.
senses: ~anheim-~ marks something as passing into another's possession or keeping.
~anheim-~ hands a matter over to someone else's judgment.
~anheim-~ lends the compound a formal, elevated register.

arm.chain: From the adjective ~arm~ ("poor"), MHG and OHG ~arm~, from Proto-West Germanic *~arm~, from Proto-Germanic *~armaz~ ("poor, wretched"). Beyond Germanic the origin is uncertain; a connection to the root behind ~Arbeit~ ("toil") and Latin ~orbus~ ("bereft") is often proposed but not secure. It is not related to the homonym ~Arm~ ("arm, limb"), which is Proto-Germanic *~armaz~ from PIE *~h₂er-~ ("to join") — the two words merged in sound only. Cognate with Dutch ~arm~, Gothic ~arms~, Swedish ~arm~.
senses: The sense of ~arm~ here is: poor, destitute, lacking.
The sense of ~arm~ here is the resultative frame: to reduce someone to poverty.

auf.chain: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under") — motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~.
senses: The prefix conveys upward motion — rising, lifting, or building up.
The prefix means "open" — undoing a closure.
The prefix conveys applying something onto a surface.
The prefix conveys using something up or consuming it entirely.
The prefix conveys emergence — arising, appearing, or beginning suddenly.
The prefix marks reconditioning or working-up — bringing something into fresh or usable condition.
The prefix marks summoning or proclaiming publicly — calling something out or calling someone forth.
The prefix marks locating — bringing something to light by searching for it.
The prefix marks impact onto a surface — motion that ends against something solid.
The prefix directs attention onto something — noticing, minding, or listening out.

aufeinander.chain: Transparently ~auf~ ("on, onto") + ~einander~ ("one another," itself ~ein~ plus the reciprocal ~ander~, "other"). It means "onto one another," and in verbal compounds it marks either physical stacking or reciprocal or successive action — ~aufeinanderlegen~ ("to lay one on top of the other"), ~aufeinanderfolgen~ ("to follow one another"). See ~auf-~ for the particle's own history.
senses: The sense of ~aufeinander-~ here is: one on top of another, stacked.
The sense of ~aufeinander-~ here is: reciprocally, upon each other.
The sense of ~aufeinander-~ here is: in succession, one after another.

aus.chain: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~.
senses: The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.
The prefix conveys thoroughness or completion — carrying an action all the way through.
The prefix conveys using something up, or extinguishing it, until nothing is left.
The prefix conveys distributing or handing out — spreading something outward among recipients.
The prefix conveys expansion or full development outward.

auseinander.chain: A transparent compound of ~aus~ ("out") and ~einander~ ("one another"), itself ~ein~ ("one") + ~ander~ ("other") — literally "out of one another," hence "apart, asunder." English builds the same idea from the same pieces in ~one another~ and ~asunder~.
senses: Marks separation: the parts end up away from each other (~auseinandernehmen~, ~auseinandergehen~).
Of people, drifting or falling apart (~sich auseinanderleben~).
Figuratively, of a text or a problem taken apart and analyzed (~sich auseinandersetzen~).

auto.chain: An incorporated noun: ~Auto~, clipped from ~Automobil~, borrowed around 1900 from French ~automobile~. That word is a hybrid coinage of the 1870s, Greek ~autós~ ("self") welded to Latin ~mobilis~ ("movable") — "self-moving" — and its mixed parentage annoyed purists in both France and Germany at the time. German clipped the Greek half and French the Latin half, which is why a German drives an ~Auto~ while a Frenchman drives an ~automobile~ and, colloquially, a ~mobile~.
senses: The sense of ~auto~ here is the noun ~Auto~ incorporated as an adverbial of means: by car.
The sense of ~auto~ here is: to travel by car (~autofahren~).

bankrott.chain: From the adjective and noun ~bankrott~, borrowed around 1500 from Italian ~banca rotta~ ("broken bench"), the ~rotta~ continuing Latin ~rupta~ ("broken"). The ~banca~ was the money-changer's trestle table at the market, the same word that gave English ~bank~; a dealer who could not pay was said to have a broken one. The picturesque claim that creditors literally smashed the table is a later embellishment, but the borrowing itself is well attested. Early German spelled it ~Panckarotta~, then ~Banquerott~ under French influence.
senses: The sense of ~bankrott~ here is: bankrupt, insolvent.
The sense of ~bankrott~ here is the resultative frame: to go bankrupt (~bankrottgehen~).

bei.chain: From MHG ~bī~, from OHG ~bī~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bī~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi~, from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). Cognate with English ~by~ and, in its unstressed form, with the English prefix ~be-~ (~become~, ~beset~): the two are one word split by stress, exactly as German split separable ~bei-~ from inseparable ~be-~.
senses: The prefix conveys placing something alongside something else, adding it to what is there.
The prefix conveys assistance — standing by or contributing to someone.
The prefix conveys joining — attaching oneself to a group or agreement.

beieinander.chain: A transparent compound adverb: the particle ~bei~ ("by, near") + ~einander~ ("one another"), itself ~ein~ + ~ander~. The sense is simply "near one another, together in one place." See the entries for ~bei~ and for the deictic adverbs it patterns with.
senses: The sense of ~beieinander-~ here is: close together, in one place.
The sense of ~beieinander-~ here is: assembled, gathered in company (~beieinandersitzen~, ~beieinanderstehen~).
The sense of ~beieinander-~ here is: kept or held together as a set.

beiseite.chain: A frozen prepositional phrase, ~bei~ + ~Seite~ ("at the side"), univerbated into a single adverb meaning "aside, out of the way." The noun ~Seite~ goes back to MHG ~sīte~, from OHG ~sīta~, and is cognate with English ~side~ and Dutch ~zijde~. In compounds such as ~beiseitelegen~ and ~beiseiteschaffen~ it names the destination of the motion: the object ends up off to one side.
senses: ~beiseite-~ moves the object off to one side, out of the way.
~beiseite-~ sets something aside for later, or removes it from view.
~beiseite-~ can imply making something disappear discreetly.

bekannt.chain: The past participle of ~bekennen~ (~be-~ + ~kennen~, "to know"), long since an ordinary adjective meaning "known, familiar". ~Kennen~ goes back to OHG ~kennen~, from Proto-Germanic *~kannijaną~, a causative of *~kunnaną~, from PIE *~ǵneh₃-~ ("to know") — so the causative sense "to make known" that ~kennen~ itself lost is exactly what ~bekanntgeben~ and ~bekanntmachen~ preserve. Cognate with Dutch ~bekend~ and archaic English ~beknown~.
senses: The sense of ~bekannt~ here is: known, familiar — the resultative state.
The sense of ~bekannt~ here is: brought into public knowledge, made generally known.

bereit.chain: From MHG ~bereite~, from OHG ~bireiti~, from Proto-West Germanic *~raidī~, from Proto-Germanic *~raidaz~ ("ready, arranged, prepared"), from PIE *~h₂rey-~ ("to count, order"). Cognate with English ~ready~, Dutch ~bereid~, Gothic ~garaiþs~ ("ordered"). As a verbal particle it is resultative: the verb puts something into a state of readiness — ~bereitstellen~, ~bereithalten~.
senses: The sense of ~bereit~ here is: into a state of readiness.
The sense of ~bereit~ here is: held available, kept on hand.
The sense of ~bereit~ here is: prepared in advance for use.

besser.chain: From ~besser~, the suppletive comparative of ~gut~: MHG ~bezzer~, OHG ~bezziro~, from Proto-Germanic *~batizô~, a comparative to the root *~bat-~ ("good, advantage"). German and English inherited the same suppletion, ~gut~/~besser~/~best~ beside ~good~/~better~/~best~, in which the comparative comes from a different root than the positive. The root also gave German ~Buße~ ("penance, amends") and ~büßen~, and English ~boot~ in the archaic ~to boot~ ("in addition"): making something better and making amends were once one idea.
senses: The sense of ~besser~ here is: better, in an improved state.
The sense of ~besser~ here is the resultative frame: to bring something into a better condition (~besserstellen~).
The sense of ~besser~ here is: claiming superior knowledge (~besserwissen~).

blank.chain: From the adjective ~blank~ ("shining, bare"), MHG ~blanc~ ("shining, white"), OHG ~blanc~, from Proto-Germanic *~blankaz~, from PIE *~bʰleg-~ ("to shine, burn") — the same root behind Latin ~flagrāre~ and, by the other half of its sense, English ~black~ ("burnt") and ~bleach~. The Germanic word was borrowed into Romance as French ~blanc~ and Italian ~bianco~, and English then took ~blank~ back from French, so German ~blank~ and English ~blank~ are one word that made a round trip. Cognate with Dutch ~blank~, Swedish ~blank~.
senses: The sense of ~blank~ here is: shining, polished, burnished.
The sense of ~blank~ here is: bare, uncovered, stripped of what usually covers it.
The sense of ~blank~ here is the resultative frame: to rub or draw something to that state (~blankputzen~, ~blankziehen~).

blau.chain: From the adjective ~blau~, MHG ~blā~, OHG ~blāo~, from Proto-Germanic *~blēwaz~, from PIE *~bʰleh₁-wos~ — cognate with Latin ~flāvus~ ("golden yellow"), one of the sharper color shifts in the family. English ~blue~ is the same Germanic word re-imported, borrowed from Old French ~bleu~, itself from Frankish. The particle's sense in ~blaumachen~ ("to skip work") is of disputed origin: it is usually traced to ~blauer Montag~, the Monday before Ash Wednesday named for the liturgical blue of Lent and later the artisans' unworked Monday, while the popular dyers' explanation — woad-dyed cloth oxidizing in the air while the dyer idled — is rejected by most linguists, and a derivation from Rotwelsch ~lau~ ("for nothing") has also been proposed.
senses: The sense of ~blau~ here is: the color blue.
The sense of ~blau~ here is: colloquially, drunk (~blau sein~).
The sense of ~blau~ here is: to skip work or school, of disputed origin (~blaumachen~).

bloß.chain: From the adjective ~bloß~ ("bare, naked"), from MHG ~blōȥ~, from OHG ~blōz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~blaut~, from Proto-Germanic *~blautaz~ ("soft, weak, bare"); the deeper origin is uncertain, possibly PIE *~bʰlew-~ ("weak"). Cognate with Dutch ~bloot~ ("bare"), Old Norse ~blautr~ ("soft, wet"), Swedish ~blott~ ("merely"), Danish ~blød~ ("soft"); English ~bloat~ is usually traced to the Old Norse relative. In verbs the adjective is resultative: ~bloßlegen~ is to lay something bare, ~bloßstellen~ to expose a person.
senses: The sense of ~bloß~ here is: bare, uncovered — the resultative state.
The sense of ~bloß~ here is: to expose to view, to lay open.
The sense of ~bloß~ here is: to expose a person, to show them up.

brach.chain: From ~Brache~ / ~brach~ ("fallow"), OHG ~brāhha~ ("the breaking up, the first plowing of a field"), an ablaut noun to Proto-Germanic *~brekan~ — the verb that is modern ~brechen~. Fallow land is thus literally broken land. The verb ~brachliegen~ grew out of the MHG phrase ~in brāche ligen~, lost its preposition in the sixteenth century and fused into one word in the nineteenth. The same noun named June: ~Brachmonat~, the month the fallow was plowed.
senses: The sense of ~brach~ here is: fallow, left uncultivated.
The sense of ~brach~ here is: unused, lying idle, of talent or capital as well as of land (~brachliegen~).

breit.chain: From the adjective ~breit~, MHG and OHG ~breit~, from Proto-West Germanic *~braid~, from Proto-Germanic *~braidaz~ ("broad"). Beyond Germanic it has no secure etymology, and the standard handbooks leave it unexplained. It is the same word as English ~broad~, which preserves the old noun in ~breadth~. Cognate with Dutch ~breed~, Gothic ~braiþs~, Swedish ~bred~.
senses: The sense of ~breit~ here is: broad, wide.
The sense of ~breit~ here is the resultative frame: to spread out, to sprawl (~sich breitmachen~).
The sense of ~breit~ here is: flattened by pressure, and figuratively talked round (~breitschlagen~).

da.chain: The deictic adverb ~da~ ("there, then"), from MHG ~dā~, from OHG ~dār~, from Proto-Germanic *~þar~, from the PIE demonstrative stem *~to-~ — the same stem behind English ~there~, ~that~, and ~the~. In verbal compounds it points at a place or situation already established in the discourse — ~dableiben~ ("to stay put"), ~dastehen~ ("to stand there"). It is the base of the large family of ~da(r)-~ compounds (~dazu~, ~davon~, ~dahin~).
senses: The sense of ~da-~ here is: there, at the place or situation already in view.
The sense of ~da-~ here is: present, on the spot.
The sense of ~da-~ here is: remaining in place rather than departing.

dabei.chain: The pronominal adverb ~da~ ("there") + ~bei~ ("by, at"), meaning "thereby, alongside it, present at it." It is transparently compositional; see the entries for ~da(r)-~ and ~bei~. In verbs such as ~dabeisein~ and ~dabeibleiben~ it locates the subject at an event rather than moving anything.
senses: ~dabei-~ places the subject at the scene, present and participating.
~dabei-~ marks continued attendance rather than motion.

dafür.chain: Transparently ~da~ ("there, it") + ~für~ ("for"): a pronominal adverb standing in for "for it, for that", since German avoids a preposition plus personal pronoun when the referent is not a person. ~Da~ is from OHG ~dār~, from the demonstrative stem that also gives ~der~ and ~das~, ultimately PIE *~tó-~. As a verbal particle it carries the sense of advocacy or substitution: ~dafürhalten~ is to be of the opinion, and the nominalized ~das Dafürhalten~ is "one's view".
senses: The sense of ~dafür-~ here is: for it, for that — the pronominal referent.
The sense of ~dafür-~ here is: in favor of, in support of something.
The sense of ~dafür-~ here is: in exchange or as a substitute for it.

dagegen.chain: Transparently ~da~ ("there, it") + ~gegen~ ("against"), a pronominal adverb for "against it, against that". ~Gegen~ is from MHG ~gegen~, OHG ~gegin~, ~gagan~ ("toward, opposite"), from Proto-Germanic *~gagin~. As a particle it is either oppositional (~dagegenhalten~, to counter; ~dagegenstimmen~, to vote against) or plainly locational (~dagegenlehnen~, to lean against it).
senses: The sense of ~dagegen-~ here is: against it, in opposition to it.
The sense of ~dagegen-~ here is: in objection or rebuttal.
The sense of ~dagegen-~ here is: leaning or resting against it.

daher.chain: The pronominal adverb ~da~ ("there") + ~her~ ("toward the speaker"), literally "from there, hither." The deictic contrast that governs this whole group is that ~her-~ points toward the speaker and ~hin-~ away from the speaker. Alongside the spatial sense it carries a causal one, "hence, therefore"; in verbs such as ~daherkommen~ and ~daherreden~ the spatial reading dominates, often with a dismissive tinge.
senses: The sense of ~daher-~ here is: motion from there toward the speaker.
The sense of ~daher-~ here is: often adds a dismissive or aimless tone to the action.
The sense of ~daher-~ here is: in its causal sense, "hence, for that reason".

dahin.chain: A transparent compound of the demonstrative ~da~ ("there") and ~hin~ ("thither, away from the speaker"), so "to that place, thither." From the spatial sense German developed a temporal one — what has gone thither is gone for good, which is why ~dahin sein~ means "to be finished, lost, done for."
senses: ~dahin-~ Marks motion toward a place already named, "there, to that point.".
Temporally, of time passing and being gone (~dahingehen~, ~dahinschwinden~).
Of a slow wasting or drifting, with no goal in view (~dahinsiechen~, ~dahinleben~).

dahinter.chain: Transparently ~da~ ("there, it") + ~hinter~ ("behind"), a pronominal adverb meaning "behind it, behind that". ~Hinter~ is from OHG ~hintar~, from Proto-Germanic *~hinder~, a comparative of the stem that also gives English ~hind~ and ~behind~. The particle is often figurative rather than spatial: ~dahinterkommen~ is to get to the bottom of something, ~dahinterstehen~ to back it.
senses: The sense of ~dahinter-~ here is: behind it, at the back of it.
The sense of ~dahinter-~ here is figuratively: at the bottom of the matter, behind the appearance.
The sense of ~dahinter-~ here is: standing behind something in support.

daneben.chain: Transparently ~da~ ("there, it") + ~neben~ ("next to"), a pronominal adverb meaning "beside it, next to that". ~Neben~ is itself a reduction of MHG ~in eben~ ("on a level with"), from OHG ~in ebani~ — the same ~eben~ as English ~even~. Beside the plain spatial sense, the particle carries a productive sense of missing the mark: ~danebengehen~ and ~danebenschießen~ are to go wide, to miss.
senses: The sense of ~daneben-~ here is: beside it, next to that.
The sense of ~daneben-~ here is: alongside, in addition to it.
The sense of ~daneben-~ here is: wide of the mark — to miss, to go wrong.

dank.chain: An incorporated noun: ~Dank~ ("thanks"), MHG ~danc~, OHG ~danc~, from Proto-Germanic *~þankaz~ ("thought, gratitude"), from PIE *~teng-~ ("to perceive, think"). The noun is thus the same word as ~Gedanke~ ("thought"), and the pair matches English ~thank~/~think~ exactly: to thank someone was to hold them in mind. In ~danksagen~ the noun stands as the incorporated object of the verb.
senses: The sense of ~dank~ here is the noun ~Dank~ incorporated as object: to render thanks.
The sense of ~dank~ here is: gratitude expressed formally or publicly (~danksagen~).

dar.chain: From OHG ~dara~ ("thither, to that place"), an extended form of OHG ~thār~/~dār~ ("there"), from Proto-West Germanic *~þār~. The directional -~r-~ marked motion toward a place, distinguishing ~dar~ ("thither") from static ~da~ ("there"). In Modern German ~dar-~ is largely fossilized, surviving as the bound form of ~da-~ before a vowel and in verbs such as ~darstellen~, ~darlegen~, ~darbieten~, and ~darbringen~, where it conveys setting something forth before an audience. English preserves the exact parallel in ~there-~ compounds such as ~therefore~ and ~thereby~.
senses: ~dar-~ presents or sets something forth before an audience.
The sense of ~dar-~ here is: directional "thither," toward that place.
The sense of ~dar-~ here is: the bound older form of ~da-~, used before a vowel.
~dar-~ offers or hands something over.

daran.chain: The pronominal adverb ~da~ ("there") + ~an~ ("on, at"), meaning "on it, at it, to it." Transparently compositional; see the entries for ~da(r)-~ and ~an~. It commonly reduces to ~dran~ in speech, and in verbs such as ~daransetzen~ and ~daranmachen~ it marks the thing to which effort is applied.
senses: ~daran-~ marks the object to which effort or attention is applied.
~daran-~ marks the setting-about of a task.
~daran-~ reduces colloquially to ~dran~.

darauf.chain: A transparent pronominal adverb: the deictic ~da~ + ~auf~, with the ~-r-~ inserted to keep the two vowels apart. It stands for "on it, on that" where English would use a preposition with a pronoun, and it also carries a temporal sense, "thereupon, next." The colloquial contraction is ~drauf~. See the entries for ~da(r)-~ and ~auf~.
senses: The sense of ~darauf-~ here is: on it, onto that.
The sense of ~darauf-~ here is: thereupon, next in sequence.
The sense of ~darauf-~ here is: arriving at an idea, hitting upon something (~daraufkommen~).

darnieder.chain: A compound adverb: the deictic ~da(r)-~ + ~nieder~ ("down"), MHG ~dânidere~ ("down there, at that lower place"). The ~dar-~ variant spread from the fifteenth century under Middle Low German influence beside the older ~danieder~, and both spellings survive. ~Nieder~ itself is Proto-Germanic *~niþar~, from PIE *~ni-~ ("down"), the same element as English ~nether~ and ~beneath~. The word is now archaic and elevated, holding on chiefly in ~darniederliegen~.
senses: The sense of ~darnieder-~ here is: down, at a lower place.
The sense of ~darnieder-~ here is: prostrate, laid low by illness or ruin (~darniederliegen~).
The sense of ~darnieder-~ here is: in a state of collapse, said of trade or morale as well as of bodies.

darunter.chain: The pronominal adverb ~darunter~, from ~da~ ("there") with the linking ~-r-~ that appears before a vowel-initial second element, plus the particle ~unter~ ("under, beneath"). Like the whole ~da(r)-~ family it refers back to something already mentioned rather than pointing at a place, so it is "under it, among them" rather than "under there." See the entries for ~da-~ and ~unter~.
senses: The sense of ~darunter-~ here is: under or beneath the thing referred to.
The sense of ~darunter-~ here is: among a group already mentioned.
The sense of ~darunter-~ here is: into a position below something.

darüber.chain: Transparently ~dar-~ + ~über~ ("over, above"), a pronominal adverb meaning "over it, about that". The ~-r-~ is not inserted: ~dar~ is the older full form, OHG ~dara~, ~dār~, and it survives precisely before vowel-initial elements (~darauf~, ~darin~, ~darum~), while bare ~da~ stands before consonants (~damit~, ~davon~). As a particle it is spatial (~darüberlegen~, to lay over) or, following ~über~'s own metaphor, topical ("about it").
senses: The sense of ~darüber-~ here is: over it, above it.
The sense of ~darüber-~ here is: about it — the topic under discussion.
The sense of ~darüber-~ here is: beyond it, in excess of that.

davon.chain: The compound adverb ~da~ ("there") + ~von~ ("from, of"), one of the ~da(r)-~ pronominal adverbs that stand in for a preposition plus a pronoun: "from that." See the ~da~ and ~von~ entries for their separate histories.
senses: In verbs ~davon-~ almost always means "away, off": movement away from a place.
With verbs of motion it usually implies escape or flight, as in running off.
In its plain pronominal use it means "of that, from that," as in speaking or living off something.

davor.chain: The pronominal adverb ~davor~, from ~da~ ("there") plus the particle ~vor~ ("before, in front of"). It is both spatial ("in front of it") and temporal ("before that, beforehand"), and like all the ~da(r)-~ adverbs it refers back to something already mentioned. See the entries for ~da-~ and ~vor~.
senses: The sense of ~davor-~ here is: in front of the thing referred to.
The sense of ~davor-~ here is: before that, beforehand.
The sense of ~davor-~ here is: positioned so as to shield or block.

dazu.chain: Transparently ~da~ ("there") + ~zu~ ("to"), one of the ~da(r)-~ pronominal adverbs that stand in for a preposition plus a pronoun: ~dazu~ is "to it, to that." In verbal compounds it means "in addition, on top of that" — ~dazugeben~ ("to add"), ~dazulernen~ ("to learn something further"), ~dazugehören~ ("to belong to it"). See ~da~ and ~zu-~.
senses: The sense of ~dazu-~ here is: to it, to that.
The sense of ~dazu-~ here is: in addition, as a further increment.
The sense of ~dazu-~ here is: belonging with what is already there.

dazwischen.chain: The pronominal adverb ~da~ ("there") + ~zwischen~ ("between"), meaning "in between, in the middle of it." ~zwischen~ goes back to OHG ~in zwiskēn~ ("between the two"), built on the numeral ~zwei~ ("two"), so the sense of twoness is still inside the word. In verbs such as ~dazwischenkommen~ and ~dazwischenreden~ it marks an intrusion into an ongoing course of events.
senses: ~dazwischen-~ intrudes into something already under way.
~dazwischen-~ positions something in the space between two others.
The sense of ~dazwischen-~ here is: often implies interruption or interference.

dicht.chain: From the adjective ~dicht~ ("dense, tight, watertight"), from MHG ~dīchte~, OHG ~dīhti~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þīhtī~, from Proto-Germanic *~þinhtaz~. The modern vowel comes from Middle Low German ~dicht~ rather than the native High German development, which surfaces as early modern ~deicht~. Cognate with Dutch ~dicht~ and English ~tight~. In verbs it is resultative or adverbial: ~dichtmachen~ is to shut something tight, ~dichthalten~ to keep a secret.
senses: The sense of ~dicht~ here is: tight, sealed — the resultative state.
The sense of ~dicht~ here is: closely, at close range.
The sense of ~dicht~ here is: shut, closed up for good.

dran.chain: The colloquial contraction of ~daran~ (~da~ + ~an~, "at it, on it"), parallel to ~drauf~ for ~darauf~ and ~drin~ for ~darin~. It is not the same reduction as ~ran~, which contracts ~heran~ and keeps that word's deictic pull toward the speaker. In verbs it belongs to the spoken register: ~drankommen~ is to have one's turn, ~dranbleiben~ to stick with something.
senses: The sense of ~dran-~ here is: at it, on it — colloquial for ~daran~.
The sense of ~dran-~ here is: in turn, up next.
The sense of ~dran-~ here is: staying with something, persisting.

drauf.chain: A colloquial contraction of ~darauf~, which is the demonstrative ~da~ ("there") plus ~auf~ ("on"), joined by the linking ~-r-~ that German inserts whenever ~da~ precedes a vowel-initial preposition (~darin~, ~darüber~, ~daran~). It is a pronominal adverb, standing in for "on it, on that" rather than naming a direction.
senses: Means "on it, onto it," pointing back at something already mentioned.
In verbs of impact it means striking down onto something (~draufschlagen~).
Spoken and informal in register; the written form is ~darauf-~.

drauflos.chain: A stacked contraction: ~darauf~ reduced to ~drauf~ ("thereupon"), plus ~los~ ("loose, off"), the inceptive particle of ~loslegen~ and ~loslaufen~. The whole marks a beginning that is heedless of consequence — ~drauflosreden~ is to start talking and keep going without thinking. It is colloquial and appears only in verbs of this heedless-onset type.
senses: ~drauflos-~ marks a heedless, unplanned beginning of the action.
~drauflos-~ implies carrying on without thought or aim.
The sense of ~drauflos-~ here is: colloquial in register.

drein.chain: A colloquial contraction of ~darein~ (~da~ + ~ein~, "into it"). In the verbs that keep it — ~dreinschauen~, ~dreinreden~ — the literal "into" sense is largely bleached: ~dreinreden~ is to talk into someone else's business, ~dreinschauen~ simply to look a certain way. See the entries for ~da-~ and ~ein~.
senses: The sense of ~drein-~ here is: into the matter at hand.
The sense of ~drein-~ here is: interfering in something already under way.
The sense of ~drein-~ here is: in ~dreinschauen~, bleached to a bare adverbial of manner.

drunter.chain: A colloquial contraction of ~darunter~ (~da~ + ~unter~, "under it"). It survives mostly in speech and in the set phrase ~drunter und drüber gehen~ ("to go every which way, to be chaos"), where the paired reduced adverbs do the work. See the entries for ~da-~ and ~unter~.
senses: The sense of ~drunter-~ here is: under the thing referred to.
The sense of ~drunter-~ here is: beneath, in the position below.
The sense of ~drunter-~ here is: in the pair ~drunter und drüber~, chaotically.

drüber.chain: A colloquial contraction of ~darüber~ (~da~ + ~über~, "over it, about it"). It is the reduced form of speech and of fixed phrases, standing to ~darüber~ as ~rüber~ stands to ~herüber~. See the entries for ~da-~ and ~über~.
senses: The sense of ~drüber-~ here is: over or above the thing referred to.
The sense of ~drüber-~ here is: across the top of something.
The sense of ~drüber-~ here is: about that matter.

durch.chain: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The deeper origin is disputed: a compound of PIE *~terh₂-~ ("to cross") with either *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see"), hence "to see across," or the enclitic *~-kʷe~ ("and"). Like ~um-~, ~durch-~ is a separability doublet — separable and stressed for literal traversal (~dúrchbrechen~, "to break in two"), inseparable for figurative penetration (~durchbréchen~, "to breach") — and the senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with English ~through~ and ~thorough~, Dutch ~door~.
senses: As a separable prefix, it conveys passage from one side to the other.
As a separable prefix, it conveys carrying an action through to completion, thoroughly.
As a separable prefix, it conveys severing — dividing something into two parts.

durcheinander.chain: Transparently ~durch~ ("through") + ~einander~ ("one another"): through one another, hence jumbled, in confusion. ~Durch~ is from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~, cognate with English ~through~. The particle is resultative — ~durcheinanderbringen~ is to muddle something, ~durcheinanderreden~ to talk over one another — and the nominalized ~das Durcheinander~ ("the mess") is the same word.
senses: The sense of ~durcheinander-~ here is: through one another — jumbled, in disorder.
The sense of ~durcheinander-~ here is: into confusion, muddled up.
The sense of ~durcheinander-~ here is: all at once, without taking turns.

ein.chain: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~.
senses: The prefix conveys inward motion — going or putting into something.
The prefix conveys inserting or incorporating something into a larger structure or category.
The prefix conveys enclosing or containing — shutting something in.
The prefix marks the onset of a state, the moment of entering into it.
The prefix marks becoming familiar through practice — repetition makes something fluent, or someone at home in it.
The prefix marks destructive collapse inward — something is stove in or falls in on itself.

einher.chain: The adverb ~ein~ (the older directional "in," as in ~einsteigen~) + ~her~ ("toward the speaker"), yielding "along, forth." It is transparently compositional and no longer used freely. In ~einhergehen~ it once described walking along in a particular manner, and the modern idiom ~einhergehen mit~ ("to go hand in hand with") extends that from gait to abstract accompaniment.
senses: The sense of ~einher-~ here is: motion along or forth, often describing manner of gait.
The sense of ~einher-~ here is in modern use, accompaniment: one thing going together with another.
The sense of ~einher-~ here is: elevated or literary in register.

eis.chain: The noun ~Eis~ ("ice"), from MHG ~īs~, from OHG ~īs~, from Proto-West Germanic *~īs~, from Proto-Germanic *~īsą~, from PIE *~h₁eyH-~ ("ice, frost"). It is incorporated as an adverbial of place: ~eislaufen~ is "to run on ice," that is, to skate. Cognate with English ~ice~, Dutch ~ijs~, Old Norse ~íss~, Swedish ~is~.
senses: The sense of ~eis~ here is: ice, the surface the action takes place on.
The sense of ~eis~ here is: in ~eislaufen~, moving on ice, skating.
The sense of ~eis~ here is: incorporated as an adverbial of place.

empor.chain: A frozen prepositional phrase: from MHG ~enbor~, ~embor~, from ~in bor~ ("into the height"), with OHG ~bor~ ("height, upper space"), a noun belonging to Proto-Germanic *~beraną~ ("to bear, carry, lift"). The ~-nb-~ assimilated to ~-mp-~, as in ~Wimper~, and the phrase hardened into a single adverb. The height, in other words, is what has been lifted up: the same root as English ~bear~ and ~birth~.
senses: ~empor-~ means upward motion, "aloft, up on high.".
It belongs to elevated and literary register; everyday German prefers ~hoch-~ or ~hinauf-~.
Figuratively it marks rising in rank, standing, or fortune.

entgegen.chain: A frozen prepositional phrase: from MHG ~engegen~, from OHG ~ingagan~, ~ingegin~, from Proto-West Germanic *~andagagin~, literally "in against," built on the element that also yields ~gegen~ ("against, toward"). Old English ~onġēan~ is the very same formation, and it is the direct ancestor of English ~again~ and ~against~.
senses: ~entgegen-~ marks motion toward something that is itself approaching: going out to meet it.
It also carries an adversarial sense — acting counter to something, opposing or contradicting it.
With verbs of giving it means "holding out toward" the person who is coming.

entlang.chain: Borrowed from Middle Low German ~entlanc~ ("along"), whose first element is the old preposition ~ant-~, ~ent-~ ("facing, opposite") that also stands in ~entgegen~, plus ~lang~ ("long"). English ~along~ is the same formation on native soil, from Old English ~andlang~ — the very same two morphemes. As a particle it is directional: ~entlanggehen~ is to walk along something, ~entlangfahren~ to drive along it.
senses: The sense of ~entlang-~ here is: along, following the length of something.
The sense of ~entlang-~ here is: alongside a line, edge, or path.

entzwei.chain: From MHG ~enzwei~, from the phrase ~in zwei~ ("in two"). The first element is the reduced preposition ~in~, not the prefix ~ent-~, though it was later respelled under that prefix's influence — a case of folk reanalysis frozen into the orthography. It is a resultative: ~entzweibrechen~ is to break something so that it ends up in two pieces. ~zwei~ is cognate with English ~two~.
senses: The sense of ~entzwei-~ here is resultative: leaves the object broken in two, in pieces.
~entzwei-~ marks the destruction as complete and irreversible.

erstauf.chain: Not a particle in its own right but a stacking of ~erst~ ("first") onto the particle ~auf~, attested only in ~erstaufführen~, which belongs beside the noun ~Erstaufführung~ ("first performance, premiere"); ~auf~ carries its ordinary sense from ~aufführen~ ("to stage, perform"). ~Erst~ is the old superlative of ~eher~ ("earlier"), the same formation as English ~erst~ and ~erstwhile~. The verb is largely confined to the infinitive and the past participle, and the stacked element is best described as this compound's own rather than as a productive particle.
senses: The sense of ~erstauf-~ here is: marking a performance as the first of its kind.
~erst~ ("first") stacked onto the particle ~auf~.
The sense of ~erstauf-~ here is: in ~erstaufführen~, staging a work for the first time.

falsch.chain: From the adjective ~falsch~ ("false, wrong"), MHG ~valsch~, OHG ~falsc~, an early borrowing directly from Latin ~falsus~ ("deceived, false"), the past participle of ~fallere~ ("to deceive"), later reinforced by Old French ~fals~. English ~false~ goes back to the same Latin word, taken up separately — one of the few adjectives the two languages borrowed from Latin independently. In verbs it is adverbial: ~falschspielen~ is to cheat at cards or to play out of tune, ~falschliegen~ to be mistaken.
senses: The sense of ~falsch~ here is: wrongly, incorrectly — adverbial.
The sense of ~falsch~ here is: deceitfully, by cheating.
The sense of ~falsch~ here is: out of tune, off key.

fehl.chain: Not the modern noun ~Fehler~ ("error") but an older adverbial ~fehl~ ("amiss, wrongly"), from the obsolete noun ~Fehl~ ("fault"), beside the verb ~fehlen~, which MHG ~vēlen~ borrowed from Old French ~faillir~, from Vulgar Latin *~fallīre~, from Latin ~fallere~ ("to deceive, disappoint"). As a free word it survives only in the fixed phrase ~fehl am Platz~; everywhere else it is bound to verbs — ~fehlschlagen~ ("to fail"), ~fehlgehen~ ("to go astray"). English ~fail~, ~fault~, ~false~, and ~fallacy~ all descend from the same Latin verb.
senses: The sense of ~fehl-~ here is: wrongly, amiss, off the mark.
The sense of ~fehl-~ here is: unsuccessfully, coming to nothing.
The sense of ~fehl-~ here is: in error, missing the intended target.

feil.chain: The archaic adjective ~feil~ ("for sale, to be had for money"), from MHG ~veile~, from OHG ~feili~, from Proto-West Germanic *~failī~. Cognate with Dutch ~veil~ and Old Norse ~falr~, and connected to Ancient Greek ~πωλέω~ (~pōléō~, "to sell") — the verb that also gives English ~monopoly~ its second half. The adjective has died out as a free word and survives only in ~feilbieten~ and ~feilhalten~, both meaning to offer goods for sale, often figuratively and disparagingly.
senses: ~feil-~ offers the object publicly for sale.
The sense of ~feil-~ here is: figuratively, sells out something that should not be for sale.
The sense of ~feil-~ here is: archaic, surviving only in these compounds.

fern.chain: From MHG ~verre~, ~verren~, from OHG ~ferro~, ~ferrana~ ("far off, from afar"), from an old Proto-Germanic locative adverb *~ferrai~, from PIE *~per-~ ("to cross, to pass through"). Cognate with English ~far~, Dutch ~ver~, Danish ~fjern~, Gothic ~fairra~. The same root, in its "through, beyond" sense, gave Latin ~per~ and Greek ~peri-~, so ~fern~ and ~perimeter~ are distant relatives — appropriately enough.
senses: The adjective means "far, distant"; the compound verb acts at or across a distance (~fernsehen~, ~fernsteuern~).
Resultative in the other direction: keeping something far off, at arm's length (~fernhalten~, ~fernbleiben~).

fertig.chain: From MHG ~vertec~, ~vertic~, from OHG ~fartīg~, derived from ~Fahrt~ ("journey") and so ultimately from ~fahren~ ("to travel"). The original sense was "ready for the journey, equipped to set out"; from "ready" it drifted to "finished, completed," which is the modern meaning. As a verbal particle it is resultative — ~fertigstellen~ ("to complete"), ~fertigmachen~ ("to get ready," colloquially "to wear out"). The old travel sense is still audible in English ~wayfaring~ and ~welfare~, built on the same Germanic root.
senses: The sense of ~fertig~ here is: into a finished, completed state.
The sense of ~fertig~ here is: ready, brought to a usable condition.
The sense of ~fertig~ here is: to the end, all the way through.

fest.chain: From the adjective ~fest~ ("firm, fixed, solid"), from MHG ~vest~, from OHG ~festi~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fastī~, from Proto-Germanic *~fastuz~, probably from PIE *~pastV-~ ("solid, stable"). Cognate with Dutch ~vast~, Swedish ~fast~, Gothic ~fastan~ ("to hold fast"), and with English ~fast~ in its older sense "firmly fixed," preserved in "hold fast" and "steadfast." English ~fast~ "quick" is that same word: to run fast was first to run hard and unwaveringly, and only later to run quickly.
senses: In a resultative compound the adjective names the end state: the action is carried on until the object is firmly fixed.
The particle adds a sense of firmness, fixedness, or permanence.
It can also mean "secured, held in place," as when something is fastened down or someone is detained.

flach.chain: From the adjective ~flach~ ("flat, level, shallow"), from MHG ~vlach~, from OHG ~flah~, from Proto-Germanic *~flakaz~, from PIE *~pleh₂k-~ ("flat, broad") — the root behind Greek ~πλάξ~ (~plax~, "flat plate") and, through it, English ~plaque~ and ~placenta~. In a resultative compound it names the end state: the action leaves its object flat. Cognate with Dutch ~vlak~, Old Norse ~flakna~ ("to flake off"), English ~flake~.
senses: The sense of ~flach~ here is: flat, level.
The sense of ~flach~ here is: leaving the object lying flat.
The sense of ~flach~ here is: shallow, not deep.

fort.chain: From MHG ~vort~, from OHG ~forth~, from Proto-West Germanic *~forþ~, from Proto-Germanic *~furþa~, from PIE *~per-~ ("forward, across") — the same root that gave ~vor-~. Cognate with English ~forth~, Dutch ~voort~.
senses: The particle conveys going away, off from a place.
The particle conveys continuation — carrying on with what was already under way.
The particle conveys onward progress.

frei.chain: From the adjective ~frei~ ("free"), from MHG ~vrī~, from OHG ~frī~, from Proto-West Germanic *~frī~, from Proto-Germanic *~frijaz~, from PIE *~preyH-~ ("to love, to be dear"). Cognate with English ~free~, Dutch ~vrij~, Danish ~fri~. The semantic bridge is a household one: the free members of a household were the beloved ones, the kin, as opposed to the slaves — and the same root gives ~Freund~ and English ~friend~.
senses: In a resultative compound ~frei-~ names the end state: the action continues until the object is free or clear.
Hence senses of clearing, exposing, or uncovering something that had been blocked.
It can also mean releasing someone or something, setting it at liberty.

fremd.chain: From the adjective ~fremd~ ("foreign, strange, not one's own"), from MHG ~vremde~, from OHG ~fremidi~, from Proto-West Germanic *~framiþī~, from Proto-Germanic *~framaþiz~, a derivative of *~fram~ ("forth, away from"). What is ~fremd~ is literally what is away, and that very adverb is the direct ancestor of English ~from~. Cognate with Dutch ~vreemd~, Swedish ~främmande~, West Frisian ~frjemd~, Gothic ~framaþeis~.
senses: The sense of ~fremd~ here is: with someone or something not one's own.
The sense of ~fremd~ here is: outside the household, the family, or the couple.
The sense of ~fremd~ here is: as a stranger, in an unfamiliar manner.

gegen.chain: The preposition ~gegen~ ("against, toward"), from MHG ~gegen~, from OHG ~gagan~, from Proto-Germanic *~gagin~. Cognate with Old Norse ~gegn~, Dutch ~tegen~, and English ~again~ and ~against~ — ~again~ originally meant "back toward, in the opposite direction," and its modern sense "once more" is a later development. As a verbal particle it supplies opposition or facing, as in ~gegenüberstehen~ and ~gegenhalten~.
senses: The sense of ~gegen-~ here is opposition: acting against something or someone.
The sense of ~gegen-~ here is: facing or confronting, positioned opposite.
The sense of ~gegen-~ here is: a counter-move answering a prior one.

gegenüber.chain: Transparently ~gegen~ ("toward, against") + ~über~ ("over") — over against, that is, facing, opposite. ~Gegen~ is from OHG ~gegin~, ~gagan~, from Proto-Germanic *~gagin~; ~über~ is from OHG ~ubar~, from PIE *~upér~, cognate with English ~over~. English once had the exact counterpart ~over against~ ("opposite"), now archaic. As a particle it is positional: ~gegenüberstehen~ is to stand facing, ~gegenüberstellen~ to confront or to juxtapose.
senses: The sense of ~gegenüber-~ here is: facing, opposite — positioned across from.
The sense of ~gegenüber-~ here is: confronting, face to face with.
The sense of ~gegenüber-~ here is: set side by side for comparison.

gerade.chain: From the adjective ~gerade~ ("straight"), whose history is genuinely tangled. MHG ~gerat~, ~gerade~ answers to OHG ~gihradi~, pointing to Proto-Germanic *~hradaz~ ("quick"), but a homophonous MHG ~gerat~ ("even", of numbers), built on ~ge-~ plus the stem of ~Rad~ ("wheel"), has clearly influenced it; etymologists differ over how much of the modern word comes from which. Both lines are still visible in the senses "straight" and "even-numbered". In verbs the "straight" sense is the live one: ~geradebiegen~ is to straighten out, ~geradestehen~ to answer for something.
senses: The sense of ~gerade~ here is: straight, unbent — the resultative state.
The sense of ~gerade~ here is: upright, erect.
The sense of ~gerade~ here is: to put right, to set straight again.

gering.chain: From the adjective ~gering~ ("slight, small"), from MHG ~geringe~, from OHG ~giringi~, ~ringi~ ("low, plain, simple, light, easy"), from Proto-Germanic *~ringwaz~ ("small, light, quick"), of uncertain origin, though possibly from PIE *~wrengʷʰ-~ ("to squeeze, wring"). Cognate with Yiddish ~גרינג~ (~gring~, "light, easy"). In verbs it supplies the low end of an evaluative scale: ~geringschätzen~ is to hold in low regard.
senses: The sense of ~gering~ here is: slight, small — the low end of a scale.
The sense of ~gering~ here is: held in low regard, disparaged.

gern.chain: From the adverb ~gern~ ("gladly, willingly"), MHG ~gerne~, OHG ~gerno~, the adverb to the lost adjective OHG ~gern~ ("eager, desirous"), from Proto-Germanic *~gernaz~, from PIE *~ǵʰer-~ ("to want, desire"). The English cognate is ~yearn~ (Old English ~giernan~), so ~gernhaben~ is at root to have something yearningly. Also cognate with Gothic ~gairns~ and with German ~begehren~ ("to covet").
senses: The sense of ~gern-~ here is: gladly, with pleasure.
The sense of ~gern-~ here is: expressing fondness or liking.
The sense of ~gern-~ here is: willingly, without reluctance.

gesund.chain: From the adjective ~gesund~ ("healthy"), from MHG ~gesunt~, from OHG ~gisunt~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gasund~, from Proto-Germanic *~sundaz~ ("healthy, unharmed") with the prefix *~ga-~. Cognate with Dutch ~gezond~ and English ~sound~ — the same word with the prefix worn away, Old English ~gesund~, surviving in the fixed phrase ~safe and sound~. In verbs the adjective is resultative: ~gesundschreiben~ is to certify someone fit, ~gesundbeten~ to heal by prayer.
senses: The sense of ~gesund~ here is: healthy, restored to health — the resultative state.
The sense of ~gesund~ here is: back to soundness, cured.
The sense of ~gesund~ here is: declared fit or well.

glatt.chain: From the adjective ~glatt~ ("smooth, slippery"), from MHG ~glat~, from OHG ~glat~ ("shining, bright, clear"), from Proto-West Germanic *~glad~, from Proto-Germanic *~gladaz~, from PIE *~ǵʰlādʰ-~, an extension of *~ǵʰel-~ ("to shine, gleam"). Cognate with Dutch ~glad~, Old Norse ~glaðr~ ("glad, bright"), Latin ~glaber~ ("smooth, hairless"), and English ~glad~ — which is the same word: Old English ~glæd~ meant "bright, shining" before it meant "cheerful", while German kept the tactile sense instead. In verbs it is resultative or adverbial: ~glattstreichen~ is to smooth out, ~glattgehen~ to come off without a hitch.
senses: The sense of ~glatt~ here is: smooth, even — the resultative state.
The sense of ~glatt~ here is: cleanly, without resistance or hitch.
The sense of ~glatt~ here is: outright, downright.

gleich.chain: From MHG ~gelīch~, from OHG ~gilīh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~galīk~, from Proto-Germanic *~galīkaz~, literally "having the same body or form": the collective prefix *~ga-~ plus the noun *~līką~ ("body, shape"). Cognate with English ~like~ and ~alike~, Dutch ~gelijk~, Old Norse ~líkr~; the English adverb suffix ~-ly~ is the same element worn down. That buried noun *~līką~ still stands on its own as German ~Leiche~ ("corpse") and in English ~lychgate~, the churchyard gate where the body was set down.
senses: The adjective means "equal, alike, the same"; the compound verb makes one thing equal to another (~gleichsetzen~, ~gleichstellen~).
Also "level, even," of surfaces and of accounts brought into balance (~ausgleichen~, ~gleichmachen~).
Of matching or measuring up to something (~gleichkommen~).

groß.chain: From MHG ~grōȥ~, from OHG ~grōȥ~ ("big, thick, coarse"), from Proto-Germanic *~grautaz~, from PIE *~gʰrewd-~ ("to grind, crush"), from *~gʰer-~ ("to rub, grind"). Cognate with Old Saxon ~grōt~, Dutch ~groot~, English ~great~. The root's older sense of coarse grinding survives in English ~groats~ and ~grits~ and in German ~Grütze~: what is "great" was first what was coarse-grained.
senses: The sense of ~groß~ here is: as a resultative adjective, "to full size", of rearing a child or animal.
The sense of ~groß~ here is: literally "large", as of writing a letter as a capital.
The sense of ~groß~ here is: figuratively "as something important", of treating or valuing.

gut.chain: The adjective ~gut~ ("good"), from MHG ~guot~, from OHG ~guot~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gōd~, from Proto-Germanic *~gōdaz~, cognate with English ~good~ and Dutch ~goed~. In these compounds it is resultative or evaluative: ~gutmachen~ is to make something good again, ~gutheißen~ to judge it good, ~gutschreiben~ to enter it on the favorable side of an account.
senses: The sense of ~gut~ here is resultative: brings the object into a good state, makes amends.
The sense of ~gut~ here is evaluative: judges or declares something good.
The sense of ~gut~ here is: in commercial use, credits to the favorable side of an account.

halt.chain: From the noun and military interjection ~Halt!~ ("stop!"), a deverbal of ~halten~ ("to hold, to stop"), from MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. ~Haltmachen~ is literally "to make a halt," the noun taken as the object of ~machen~. English ~halt~ in the military sense is the same word, borrowed by way of French ~halte~, which French had itself taken from German.
senses: The sense of ~halt~ here is: a stop, a halt.
The sense of ~halt~ here is: coming to a stop, breaking off movement.
The sense of ~halt~ here is: in ~haltmachen~, making a halt.

haus.chain: The noun ~Haus~ ("house"), from MHG ~hūs~, from OHG ~hūs~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hūs~, from Proto-Germanic *~hūsą~, of uncertain further origin — possibly from PIE *~(s)kew-~ ("to cover, conceal"), though this is not secure. It is incorporated as the object of the verb: ~haushalten~ is "to hold house," to keep house and, by extension, to economize. Cognate with English ~house~, Dutch ~huis~, Old Norse ~hús~, Swedish ~hus~.
senses: The sense of ~haus~ here is: the house or household.
The sense of ~haus~ here is: in ~haushalten~, keeping house and managing resources.
The sense of ~haus~ here is: incorporated as the object of the verb.

heilig.chain: From the adjective ~heilig~ ("holy, sacred"), MHG ~heilec~, OHG ~heilag~, from Proto-Germanic *~hailagaz~, a derivative of *~hailaz~ ("whole, sound, uninjured") — modern German ~heil~. The same stem gives English ~whole~, ~hale~, ~heal~, and ~holy~: in Germanic, holiness and wholeness are one idea, and what is sacred is what is intact. In a resultative compound it names the state conferred, as in ~heiligsprechen~ ("to canonize," literally "to speak holy").
senses: The sense of ~heilig~ here is: holy, sacred.
The sense of ~heilig~ here is: declaring or making something holy.
The sense of ~heilig~ here is: resulting in sanctified status.

heim.chain: From the noun ~Heim~ ("home"), used in verbs as the old adverbial accusative of direction, "homeward." From MHG ~heim~, from OHG ~heim~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haim~, from Proto-Germanic *~haimaz~ ("home, village"), from PIE *~ḱóymos~ ("settlement, home"). Cognate with English ~home~, Dutch ~heem~, Swedish ~hem~; the same root surfaces in Latin ~cīvis~ ("citizen"), one who belongs to a settlement.
senses: ~heim-~ means "home, homeward": the verb's action is directed back to the home.
It is a bare directional adverb, not a preposition, which is why it takes no article and governs no case.
By extension it can mean returning to one's own country or place of origin.

heiß.chain: From the adjective ~heiß~ ("hot"), MHG ~heiȥ~, OHG ~heiȥ~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hait~, from Proto-Germanic *~haitaz~. As a resultative it names the end state: ~heißlaufen~ is to run until hot, to overheat. Cognate with English ~hot~ and ~heat~, Dutch ~heet~, Old Norse ~heitr~, Swedish ~het~. Despite the near-identity of the modern forms, this adjective is generally held to be unrelated to the verb ~heißen~ ("to be called"), which goes back to Proto-Germanic *~haitaną~.
senses: The sense of ~heiß~ here is: hot.
The sense of ~heiß~ here is: resulting in the object becoming hot.
The sense of ~heiß~ here is: running or working until overheated.

hell.chain: From the adjective ~hell~ ("bright, light"), from MHG ~hel~, which meant "resounding, loud" before it meant "shining" — the word began as a term of hearing and crossed over to sight. It belongs to OHG ~hellan~ ("to resound"), the source of modern ~hallen~ ("to echo") and ~Hall~ ("reverberation"), from PIE *~kelh₁-~ ("to call, shout"), the root also behind Latin ~calāre~ and Greek ~καλέω~ (~kaléō~, "I call"). German still keeps both channels: a ~helle Stimme~ is a high clear voice and a ~helles Zimmer~ a well-lit room.
senses: The sense of ~hell~ here is: bright, full of light.
The sense of ~hell~ here is: resulting in something becoming bright or clear.
The sense of ~hell~ here is: clear and undimmed, of sound or of perception.

her.chain: From MHG ~her~, from OHG ~hera~, belonging to the Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~ ("this, here"), from PIE *~ḱi-~ ("this, here") — the same stem that yields ~hier~ and ~heute~ ("this day"). Cognate with English ~here~ and, through the same demonstrative, English ~he~.
senses: ~her-~ marks motion toward the speaker — "hither" — and is the exact counterpart of ~hin-~, which marks motion away from the speaker. This opposition is the organizing fact of the whole deictic group.
The sense of ~her-~ here is: It can also point backward in time, meaning "from then until now.".
It is the first element of the compound particles ~heraus~, ~herein~, ~herunter~, ~herum~, ~heran~, ~herüber~, and of their colloquial contractions ~raus~, ~rein~, ~runter~, ~rum~, ~ran~, ~rüber~.

herab.chain: A transparent compound of ~her-~ ("hither," marking motion toward the speaker, from OHG ~hera~, from the Proto-Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~, from PIE *~ḱi-~ "this") and ~ab~ ("off, down"), so "downward and toward the speaker" — the motion seen from below. Its mirror image is ~hinab~, the same descent away from the speaker.
senses: Marks downward motion oriented toward the speaker or the vantage point below.
Figuratively, of condescension or disparagement, looking down on someone (~herabsehen~, ~herabsetzen~).

heran.chain: The compound adverb ~her~ ("toward the speaker") + ~an~ ("on, at, up to"); see those entries for their separate histories. Colloquially it contracts to ~ran~.
senses: ~heran-~ means approaching: coming up to the speaker or to a point of reference.
With transitive verbs it means bringing something nearer.
Figuratively it marks taking on a task, or growing up toward a standard.

herauf.chain: A transparent compound of ~her-~ ("hither," marking motion toward the speaker, from OHG ~hera~, from the Proto-Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~, from PIE *~ḱi-~ "this") and ~auf~ ("up, onto"), so "upward and toward the speaker." Its mirror image is ~hinauf~, the same motion away from the speaker.
senses: Marks upward motion oriented toward the speaker or the vantage point.
Also of time and weather moving in on one (~heraufziehen~, of a storm).

heraus.chain: Transparently ~her-~ ("hither, toward the speaker") plus ~aus~ ("out"), hence "out toward the speaker" — the mirror of ~hinaus~, "out away from the speaker." This her/hin opposition is the single most useful fact about the whole deictic group. Colloquial German contracts ~heraus~ to ~raus~. See the entries for ~her-~ and ~aus-~.
senses: The particle conveys outward motion toward the speaker.
The particle conveys bringing something out into the open — publishing, discovering, or making public.

herbei.chain: A transparent compound of ~her-~ ("hither," marking motion toward the speaker, from OHG ~hera~, from the Proto-Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~, from PIE *~ḱi-~ "this") and ~bei~ ("by, near"), so "hither, to this spot" — motion that ends up close to the speaker. Unlike the other ~her-~ compounds it names no axis, only arrival at the near point.
senses: ~herbei-~ Marks motion up to the speaker, "over here, near.".
Often of summoning or fetching something so that it is at hand (~herbeirufen~, ~herbeischaffen~).

herein.chain: A transparent compound of ~her-~ ("hither," marking motion toward the speaker, from OHG ~hera~, from the Proto-Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~, from PIE *~ḱi-~ "this") and ~ein~ ("in, into"), so "inward and toward the speaker" — the movement of someone entering the room one is standing in. Its mirror image is ~hinein~, the same motion away from the speaker.
senses: Marks inward motion oriented toward the speaker.
Figuratively, of drawing someone into a situation, often an unwelcome one (~hereinlegen~, "to take in, to dupe").

herum.chain: The compound adverb ~her~ ("toward the speaker") + ~um~ ("around"); see those entries for their separate histories. In everyday speech it contracts to ~rum~.
senses: ~herum-~ conveys motion around or about something, whether encircling it or milling about within it.
With verbs of activity it often adds an aimless, idle sense — fiddling about rather than getting anywhere.
It can also mean simply "the other way around," of turning or reversing something.

herunter.chain: The compound adverb ~her~ ("toward the speaker") + ~unter~ ("under"); see those entries for their separate histories. Colloquially it contracts to ~runter~.
senses: ~herunter-~ means downward motion toward the speaker: down from up there to here.
Its counterpart ~hinunter-~ traces the same downward path away from the speaker.
By extension it means reducing something — bringing a price, a volume, or a fever down.

hervor.chain: A transparent compound of ~her-~ ("hither," marking motion toward the speaker, from OHG ~hera~, from the Proto-Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~, from PIE *~ḱi-~ "this") and ~vor~ ("before, in front," from OHG ~fora~, from PIE *~per-~ "forward, in front"), together "forth and toward the speaker" — out from behind or beneath something, into view.
senses: ~hervor-~ Marks emergence into view, "forth, out from.".
Figuratively, of something standing out or being brought to notice (~hervorheben~, ~hervorragen~).

herüber.chain: The deictic adverb ~her-~ plus the particle ~über~ ("over, across"): motion across and toward the speaker. ~Her-~ points toward the speaker and ~hin-~ away from the speaker — the single fact that unlocks this whole family — so ~herüber~ is "over to this side" and ~hinüber~ "over to that one." Colloquially contracted to ~rüber~. See the entries for ~her-~ and ~über~.
senses: The sense of ~herüber-~ here is: across, toward the speaker.
The sense of ~herüber-~ here is: over to this side.
The sense of ~herüber-~ here is: from there to here.

hier.chain: The adverb ~hier~ ("here"), from MHG ~hier~, from OHG ~hier~, from Proto-Germanic *~hēr~, formed to the demonstrative stem *~hi-~ ("this"), from PIE *~ḱe-~ ("this, here"). As a particle it simply fixes the action at the speaker's location, as in ~hierbleiben~ ("to stay here"). Cognate with English ~here~, Dutch ~hier~, Old Norse ~hér~, Gothic ~hēr~; the same demonstrative stem sits inside English ~he~ and German ~heute~, originally "on this day."
senses: The sense of ~hier-~ here is: here, at this place.
The sense of ~hier-~ here is: fixing the action at the speaker's location.
The sense of ~hier-~ here is: staying or remaining put.

hierher.chain: The adverb ~hier~ ("here") compounded with the deictic ~her~ ("hither"): literally "here-hither". Like the rest of the ~her-~ / ~hin-~ family it is transparently compositional — ~her-~ points motion toward the speaker, ~hin-~ away from the speaker — and its etymology is that of its two parts.
senses: The sense of ~hierher-~ here is: directional, "to this place, over here".
The sense of ~hierher-~ here is: with verbs of motion or transport, "toward the speaker's location".

hin.chain: From OHG ~hina~, from Proto-Germanic *~hina~ ("away from here, thither"), from the PIE demonstrative stem *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"). ~Hin-~ points away from the speaker and ~her-~ toward the speaker; English once drew the same line with ~thither~ and ~hither~. Cognate with English ~hence~ and ~here~.
senses: The particle indicates motion away from the speaker, toward some other place.
The particle conveys setting something down in a particular place.
The particle conveys motion toward a destination, paired against ~her-~ for motion toward the speaker.

hinab.chain: The deictic adverb ~hin~ ("thither, away from the speaker") compounded with ~ab~ ("off, down"): motion downward and away. Transparently compositional; the etymology belongs to the two component entries, and the deictic contrast is with ~herab~ ("down toward the speaker").
senses: The sense of ~hinab-~ here is: directional, "down, downward".
The sense of ~hinab-~ here is: with the deictic sense "away from the speaker", against ~herab~.

hinauf.chain: A transparent compound of ~hin-~ ("thither," marking motion away from the speaker) and ~auf~ ("up, onto"), so "upward and away from the speaker" — the climb seen from the bottom. Its mirror image is ~herauf~, the same ascent toward the speaker.
senses: Marks upward motion oriented away from the speaker.
Also of extending a scale or a stretch upward (~hinaufsetzen~, of prices).

hinaus.chain: The compound adverb ~hin~ ("away from the speaker") + ~aus~ ("out"); see the ~her~ entry for the deictic pair. Colloquially it contracts to ~raus~, a contraction it shares with ~heraus~.
senses: ~hinaus-~ means motion out of something, directed away from the speaker.
Its counterpart ~heraus-~ traces the same outward path toward the speaker: the one inside goes ~hinaus~, and the one already outside watches him come ~heraus~.
With expressions of time or measure it means "beyond," going past a limit.

hindurch.chain: The deictic adverb ~hin-~ plus the particle ~durch~ ("through"): motion through something and away from the speaker. ~Hin-~ points away from the speaker and ~her-~ toward the speaker; ~hindurch~ therefore traces a path all the way out the far side, and it is used of stretches of time endured from end to end as readily as of space. See the entries for ~hin-~ and ~durch~.
senses: The sense of ~hindurch-~ here is: through and out the far side.
The sense of ~hindurch-~ here is: away from the speaker, passing through something.
The sense of ~hindurch-~ here is: throughout, from beginning to end.

hinein.chain: The compound adverb ~hin~ ("away from the speaker") + ~ein~ ("in"); see the ~her~ entry for the deictic pair. ~Hin~ comes from MHG ~hin~, from OHG ~hina~, from the same Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~ that gives ~her~ and ~hier~. Colloquially it contracts to ~rein~, a contraction it shares with ~herein~.
senses: ~hinein-~ means motion into something, directed away from the speaker.
Its counterpart ~herein-~ traces the same inward path toward the speaker: the one outside goes ~hinein~, and the one already inside watches him come ~herein~.
Figuratively it marks throwing oneself into an activity or a situation.

hintan.chain: A fossilized adverb, no longer used on its own. It arose in MHG by univerbation of ~hin~ + ~dan~ (an older local form of ~dann~), and was afterwards reanalyzed as ~hint~ — a variant of today's ~hinten~, "at the back" — plus ~an~, a folk etymology that stuck. It means "to the rear, out of the way," and survives only in a small set of elevated, faintly bureaucratic verbs: ~hintanstellen~ and ~hintansetzen~ ("to set aside, subordinate"), ~hintanhalten~ ("to hold off").
senses: The sense of ~hintan-~ here is: to the rear, set behind other things.
The sense of ~hintan-~ here is: subordinated, given lower priority.
The sense of ~hintan-~ here is: held off, kept at a distance.

hinterher.chain: Transparently ~hinter~ ("behind") + ~her~, the deictic adverb of motion toward the speaker or reference point. It means "behind, after" in space and "afterwards" in time — ~hinterherlaufen~ ("to run after"), ~hinterherfahren~ ("to drive along behind"). The deictic contrast that organizes this whole family is ~her-~ toward the speaker versus ~hin-~ away from the speaker. See ~hinter-~ and ~her-~.
senses: The sense of ~hinterher-~ here is: behind, following after in space.
The sense of ~hinterher-~ here is: afterwards, subsequently in time.
The sense of ~hinterher-~ here is: in pursuit of, trailing someone or something.

hinunter.chain: A transparent compound of ~hin-~ ("thither," marking motion away from the speaker) and ~unter~ ("under, below"), so "downward and away from the speaker" — the descent seen from above. Its mirror image is ~herunter~, the same descent toward the speaker; colloquial ~runter~ replaces both.
senses: Marks downward motion oriented away from the speaker.
Of swallowing, the food goes down and away (~hinunterschlucken~).

hinweg.chain: A transparent compound of ~hin-~ ("thither," marking motion away from the speaker) and ~weg~ ("away"), the two elements reinforcing each other: motion off and away, with no return implied. The stress distinguishes the particle ~hinwég-~ from the noun-derived adverb ~Hínweg~ ("the way there").
senses: Marks motion away and off, over and past something.
Figuratively, of overriding or brushing aside an obstacle or an objection (~sich hinwegsetzen~, ~hinwegtäuschen~).

hinzu.chain: The deictic adverb ~hin~ ("away from the speaker") + ~zu~ ("to, toward"), yielding "to it in addition." The orientation contrast is the key fact for this whole group: ~hin-~ points away from the speaker, ~her-~ toward the speaker. In ~hinzufügen~ and ~hinzukommen~ the sense is additive rather than spatial: something joins what is already there.
senses: The sense of ~hinzu-~ here is additive: joins something to what is already present.
The sense of ~hinzu-~ here is: motion toward a goal away from the speaker.

hoch.chain: Not a prefix but the adjective ~hoch~ ("high") used adverbially, from MHG ~hōch~, from OHG ~hōh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hauh~, from Proto-Germanic *~hauhaz~, from PIE *~kewk-~ ("to elevate"). Cognate with English ~high~, Dutch ~hoog~, Swedish ~hög~, Gothic ~hauhs~.
senses: The adverb conveys upward motion — the base verb performed in an upward direction.
The adverb conveys raising something to a higher position.
The adverb is the everyday spoken counterpart of ~auf-~ or of literary ~empor-~.

inne.chain: An old adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, meaning "within, inside," from OHG ~inne~/~inna~, cognate with Old Saxon ~inna~ and Old Norse ~inni~. It is no longer a free word and survives bound in ~innehalten~ ("to pause"), ~innewerden~ ("to become aware"), ~innehaben~ ("to hold an office"), and ~innewohnen~ ("to be inherent in"). English shows the same adverb nominalized in ~inn~, originally simply the place one is in.
senses: The sense of ~inne-~ here is: inward or internal location rather than motion.
The sense of ~inne-~ here is: with verbs of perception, coming to inward awareness.
The sense of ~inne-~ here is: with ~halten~, a holding-in that reads as pausing.
~inne-~ marks something as held or contained within.

irre.chain: The adjective and adverb ~irre~ ("astray, confused"), from MHG ~irre~, from OHG ~irri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~irrī~, from Proto-Germanic *~irzijaz~ ("bewildered, lost"), from PIE *~h₁ers-~ ("to wander"). Cognate with Gothic ~airzeis~ and, through the same PIE root, with Latin ~errāre~ — so ~irreführen~ and English ~err~, ~error~, ~erratic~, and the ~errant~ of ~knight-errant~ all descend from one root meaning "to wander off." As a particle it puts the object into a state of error.
senses: ~irre-~ leads the object astray, into error.
The sense of ~irre-~ here is: with ~werden~, losing one's bearings or one's faith in something.
~irre-~ implies deliberate deception when the agent is a person.

kalt.chain: From the adjective ~kalt~ ("cold"), MHG ~kalt~, OHG ~kalt~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kald~, from Proto-Germanic *~kaldaz~, originally a participle to *~kalaną~ ("to be cold"), from PIE *~gel-~ ("cold, to freeze"). As a resultative it names the end state, and figuratively the coldness is social: ~kaltstellen~ is to put a rival on ice. Cognate with English ~cold~ and ~chill~, Dutch ~koud~, Old Norse ~kaldr~, Gothic ~kalds~; the same PIE root gives Latin ~gelū~, and through it English ~gelid~ and Italian ~gelato~.
senses: The sense of ~kalt~ here is: cold.
The sense of ~kalt~ here is: resulting in the object becoming cold.
The sense of ~kalt~ here is: figuratively, freezing someone out or sidelining them.

kaputt.chain: Borrowed in the 17th century from French ~capot~ in the phrases ~faire capot~, ~être capot~ — a term from the card game piquet, where to be ~capot~ is to have taken no trick at all. Soldiers of the Thirty Years' War carried ~capot machen~ into German as ~kaputt machen~, and the card-table sense of "utterly beaten" hardened into "broken, ruined." The further origin of French ~capot~ is uncertain: Pfeifer suggests a figurative use of ~capot~ ("hood"), a hood pulled over the head leaving one helpless, while others route it through the nautical ~capoter~ ("to capsize") — the popular derivation straight from Latin ~caput~ ("head") is at best indirect. German then lent the word back out: English ~kaput~ and Dutch ~kapot~ are borrowings from it.
senses: Resultative: the verb breaks something, leaving it broken (~kaputtmachen~, ~kaputtschlagen~).
Of people, worn out or exhausted rather than literally broken (~sich kaputtarbeiten~, ~sich kaputtlachen~).
Colloquial throughout; the neutral standard verbs are ~zerbrechen~ and ~zerstören~.

kehrt.chain: From the military command ~Kehrt!~ ("about face!"), the imperative of ~kehren~ ("to turn"), from MHG ~kēren~, from OHG ~kēran~, of uncertain PIE origin. ~Kehrtmachen~ is literally "to make an about-face" — to turn on one's heel and go back the way one came, on the parade ground or in an argument. The same stem gives ~Kehrtwendung~ ("about-face, U-turn") and ~umkehren~ ("to turn around, to return").
senses: The sense of ~kehrt-~ here is: about face, turning to face the opposite way.
The sense of ~kehrt-~ here is: turning back the way one came.
The sense of ~kehrt-~ here is: reversing course, literally or figuratively.

klar.chain: From MHG ~klār~ ("bright, pure"), borrowed from Latin ~clārus~ ("bright, clear, distinct"), which also gave English ~clear~, ~clarity~, and ~declare~. In verbal compounds it is a resultative adjective: the verb brings its object into a clear state. The Latin adjective originally meant "loud, ringing," from PIE *~kelh₁-~ ("to call"), and shifted from hearing to sight before German borrowed it.
senses: The sense of ~klar~ here is: into a clear or settled state.
The sense of ~klar~ here is: so that something becomes plain and unambiguous.
The sense of ~klar~ here is: resolving what was murky or unfinished.

klein.chain: From MHG ~kleine~ ("fine, delicate, dainty"), from OHG ~kleini~ ("fine, elegant, shining"), from Proto-West Germanic *~klainī~, from Proto-Germanic *~klainiz~; the PIE source is uncertain, possibly *~gleh₁y-~ ("to stick, to smear"). Cognate with Dutch ~klein~ and — the surprise — English ~clean~: the two are doublets, English keeping the "pure, unsoiled" end of the old "bright, fine" sense while German took the "delicate" end and narrowed it to "small," displacing older ~lützel~, the cognate of English ~little~.
senses: Resultative: the verb reduces something to small pieces (~kleinschneiden~, ~kleinhacken~, ~kleinmahlen~).
Figuratively, of cutting a person or a claim down to size (~kleinreden~, ~kleinkriegen~).

klug.chain: From MHG ~kluoc~, borrowed in the mid-twelfth century from Middle Low German ~klōk~ and Middle Dutch ~cloec~ and spreading inland from the Lower Rhine; the ultimate origin is uncertain. The oldest attested sense is "strong, brave, dexterous," which shifted to "clever, shrewd, sensible." A proposed link to PIE *~gel-~ ("to ball up") is generally judged unlikely. Cognate with Dutch ~kloek~ ("stout, capable") and Low German ~klook~.
senses: The sense of ~klug~ here is: the adjective ~klug~ ("clever, wise") as the state the action produces.
The sense of ~klug~ here is: often ironic, of talk that merely sounds wise.

krank.chain: From MHG ~kranc~ ("weak, slender, slight"), from OHG *~krank~, from Proto-West Germanic *~krank~, from Proto-Germanic *~krangaz~, *~krankaz~ ("bent, weak"). Cognate with English ~crank~, Dutch ~krank~. The modern sense "ill" is a late medieval shift: MHG's ordinary word for "sick" was ~siech~, cognate with English ~sick~, and ~krank~ pushed outward from "weak" until it displaced it. As a verbal particle it is resultative — ~krankschreiben~ ("to sign someone off sick"), ~sich krankmelden~.
senses: The sense of ~krank~ here is: into a state of illness.
The sense of ~krank~ here is: declared or registered as sick.
The sense of ~krank~ here is: weakened, impaired.

kund.chain: From MHG ~kunt~, from OHG ~kund~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kunþ~, from Proto-Germanic *~kunþaz~, originally the past participle of *~kunnaną~ ("to know"), from PIE *~ǵneh₃-~ ("to know"). The modern adjective is thus a fossilized participle: ~kund~ stands to ~können~ roughly as English archaic ~couth~ stands to ~can~ — and of that pair only the negative ~uncouth~ is still in daily use. Related to English ~can~, ~know~ and ~ken~.
senses: The sense of ~kund-~ here is: as an incorporated adjective, "known", giving the verb the sense "to make known, announce".
The sense of ~kund-~ here is: in the formal register of proclamations and public notices.

kurz.chain: The adjective ~kurz~ ("short"), from MHG ~kurz~, from OHG ~kurz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kurt~, borrowed from Latin ~curtus~ ("cut short"), from PIE *~(s)ker-~ ("to cut") — the root behind English ~shear~, ~short~, ~shirt~, and ~skirt~. As a verbal particle it is resultative or manner-adverbial: ~kurzschließen~ closes a circuit by the short path, ~kurzhalten~ keeps someone on a short rein.
senses: The sense of ~kurz~ here is resultative: makes or leaves the object short.
The sense of ~kurz~ here is: by the short route, bypassing what lies between.
~kurz~ keeps something sparing or restricted.

kürzer.chain: The comparative of the adjective ~kurz~, from MHG ~kurz~, from OHG ~kurz~, an early borrowing of Latin ~curtus~ ("shortened, cut off") that displaced the inherited Germanic word. English ~curt~ is a later, direct borrowing of the same Latin adjective; English ~short~ is a relative rather than a descendant, from Proto-Germanic *~skurtaz~. Cognate with Dutch ~kort~, Danish ~kort~.
senses: The sense of ~kürzer~ here is: the comparative ~kürzer~ ("shorter"), framing the action as a reduction.
The sense of ~kürzer~ here is: figuratively, of scaling back or easing off.

lahm.chain: From MHG ~lam~, from OHG ~lam~, from Proto-West Germanic *~lam~, from Proto-Germanic *~lamaz~ ("lame, crippled"), probably from a PIE root *~lem-~ ("to break"). Cognate with English ~lame~, Dutch ~lam~, Old Norse ~lami~, Swedish ~lam~. In resultative compounds it names the endpoint: to lay something lame is to bring it to a standstill.
senses: The sense of ~lahm~ here is: the adjective ~lahm~ ("lame, paralyzed") as the resulting state.
The sense of ~lahm~ here is: figuratively, brought to a standstill or rendered inoperative.

lang.chain: From MHG ~lanc~, from OHG ~lang~, from Proto-West Germanic *~lang~, from Proto-Germanic *~langaz~, from PIE *~dlongʰos~ ("long"). Cognate with English ~long~, Dutch ~lang~, Latin ~longus~. As a separable element it is an ordinary adjective in a resultative or extent-denoting frame.
senses: The sense of ~lang~ here is: as a resultative adjective, "to (a greater) length".
The sense of ~lang~ here is: of duration, "for a long time".
The sense of ~lang~ here is: with verbs of motion, "along".

leer.chain: From MHG ~lǣre~, ~lēr~, from OHG ~lāri~ ("empty, bare"), from Proto-West Germanic *~lāʀi~, from Proto-Germanic *~lēziz~. Cognate with Dutch ~laar~ and Bavarian ~lar~; there is no surviving English relative, and the origin beyond Germanic is uncertain. DWDS derives it from the preterite-plural stem of ~lesen~ ("to gather, glean"), which would make the original sense "gleaned over" — a harvested field left open to the poor — and only later "containing nothing".
senses: The sense of ~leer~ here is as a resultative adjective, "empty": the verb acts until nothing is left.
The sense of ~leer~ here is: of a container or space, "to emptiness".
The sense of ~leer~ here is: of a machine or engine, "without load, idling".

leicht.chain: From MHG ~līht(e)~, from OHG ~līht~, from Proto-West Germanic *~līht~, from Proto-Germanic *~linhtaz~, from PIE *~h₁lengʷʰ-~ ("light, not heavy"). Cognate with English ~light~ (not heavy), Dutch ~licht~, Danish ~let~, Latin ~levis~. The same root names the lungs — German ~Lunge~, English ~lung~ — the organ that floats when the rest of the carcass sinks.
senses: The sense of ~leicht~ here is: the adjective ~leicht~ ("light, easy") as the resulting state.
The sense of ~leicht~ here is: of making something easier or less burdensome.

locker.chain: First recorded in Early New High German as ~loger~ in the fifteenth century, a Central German form beside MHG ~lücke~, ~lugge~ ("loose"), which survives dialectally as Upper German ~luck~ and Swiss ~lugg~; the ~-er~ is the suffix of ~bitter~, ~lauter~, ~munter~. Probably related to ~Lücke~ ("gap") and ~Loch~ ("hole"), but secure cognates outside German are lacking. The verb ~lockern~ was formed from the adjective only in the eighteenth century.
senses: The sense of ~locker~ here is: the adjective ~locker~ ("loose, slack") as the resulting state.
The sense of ~locker~ here is: of slackening a grip or hold, hence figuratively of giving in.

los.chain: From the adjective ~los~ ("loose, free, unattached"), from MHG ~lōs~, from OHG ~lōs~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laus~, from Proto-Germanic *~lausaz~, probably from PIE *~lewH-~ ("to cut off, loosen"). Cognate with English ~loose~ and Dutch ~los~. The German suffix ~-los~ and the English suffix ~-less~ are this same adjective, worn down into a bound ending.
senses: The sense of ~los-~ here is As a particle ~los-~ most often marks inception: ~loslaufen~ is not "to run loose" but "to start running.".
It also keeps its literal adjectival sense of releasing, loosening, or detaching something.
