It can mark separation from a fixed point, of a vehicle or a rope being let go.
The sense of ~los-~ here is As a bare imperative, ~los!~ survives on its own: "go, get on with it.".

madig.chain: From the noun ~Made~ ("maggot") plus the adjective suffix ~-ig~, hence "full of maggots, maggot-eaten." ~Made~ goes back to MHG ~made~, OHG ~mado~, from Proto-West Germanic *~maþō~, from Proto-Germanic *~maþô~. Cognate with Old English ~maþa~, Dutch ~made~, Gothic ~maþa~; English ~maggot~ and ~mawkish~ (originally "maggoty") belong to the same family through Old Norse ~maðkr~. The resultative is vivid: to make a thing maggoty in someone's eyes is to spoil it for them.
senses: The sense of ~madig~ here is: the adjective ~madig~ ("maggoty, worm-eaten") as the resulting state.
The sense of ~madig~ here is: figuratively, of spoiling something for someone by running it down.

mal.chain: From the noun ~Mal~ ("time, instance"), from MHG ~māl~ ("point in time, mark"), from OHG ~māl~, from Proto-Germanic *~mēlą~, from PIE *~meh₁-~ ("to measure"). Cognate with Gothic ~mēl~ ("time"), Dutch ~maal~, and English ~meal~, which began as "an appointed time" and only later meant the food eaten at one — the older sense survives in ~piecemeal~. The noun is incorporated adverbially from arithmetic's ~drei mal vier~: to take a number a given number of times.
senses: The sense of ~mal~ here is: the noun ~Mal~ ("time, instance") incorporated adverbially.
The sense of ~mal~ here is: in arithmetic, "times" — hence to multiply.

matt.chain: Two borrowings that fell together. The sense "weak, exhausted, dull" is MHG ~mat~ (thirteenth century), most likely from Old French ~mat~ ("defeated, downcast"). The chess sense arrived around 1200 in the phrase ~schāch unde mat~, from Old French ~mat~, from Arabic ~māt~ ("he is dead"), the second word of Persian ~šāh māt~ — the king is helpless. English ~checkmate~ is the same phrase, and the verbal use preserves that sharper sense: to leave an opponent no move.
senses: The sense of ~matt~ here is: the adjective ~matt~ ("weak, dull, listless") as the resulting state.
The sense of ~matt~ here is: in chess, "checkmated" — hence to outmaneuver an opponent completely.

maus.chain: An intensifier of disputed origin, familiar from ~mausetot~ ("stone dead"). It looks like ~Maus~ ("mouse"), and speakers have long read it that way, but the older Low German form is ~mūsdōd~ beside ~mursdōd~, ~morsdōd~ ("quite dead"), which points to a Low German intensifying element perhaps connected with ~morsch~ ("rotten") rather than to the animal. The mouse reading is probably a folk etymology, encouraged by the equally intensifying ~mäuschenstill~. Either way, its work in a compound is purely emphatic.
senses: The sense of ~maus-~ here is an intensifier: "utterly, stone-".
The sense of ~maus-~ here is: outwardly the noun ~Maus~ ("mouse"), though that identification is likely secondary.

maß.chain: The noun ~Maß~ ("measure, moderation"), from MHG ~māȥe~, from OHG ~māȥa~, a derivative of ~messen~ ("to measure"), from Proto-Germanic *~metaną~, from PIE *~med-~ ("to measure, to take appropriate measures"). It is incorporated as the verb's object: ~maßhalten~ is literally "to hold measure", while ~maßregeln~ is denominal from ~Maßregel~ ("regulation"). The same root gives English ~mete~ and, through Latin, ~moderate~ and ~modest~ — words that keep ~Maß~'s second sense of restraint.
senses: The sense of ~maß~ here is: the incorporated noun "measure", standing as the verb's object.
The sense of ~maß~ here is: in the extended sense "moderation, restraint".
The sense of ~maß~ here is: in formations built on ~Maßregel~ ("regulation"), yielding "to discipline, reprimand".

mit.chain: From MHG ~mit(e)~, from OHG ~mit~, ~miti~, from Proto-West Germanic *~midi~, from Proto-Germanic *~midi~ ("with, among"), from PIE *~me~ ("in the middle of, near"). Cognate with English ~mid~ — still visible in ~amid~ and in ~midwife~, literally "with-woman," one who is with the mother — and with Greek ~metá~ ("with, after").
senses: The prefix conveys accompaniment — going along with someone or bringing something along.
The prefix conveys participation — taking part in something others are doing.
The prefix conveys inclusion — doing something too, in addition to the rest.

mobil.chain: Borrowed from French ~mobile~, from Latin ~mōbilis~ ("movable," from *~movibilis~, to ~movēre~ "to move"). The German military use dates from about 1800 and keeps the literal sense: to put troops on a war footing is to make them movable. Its doublet is ~Möbel~ — French ~meuble~, from Latin ~mōbilia~ ("movable goods") — so furniture is etymologically the property one could carry away. Cognate with English ~mobile~, ~mobilize~.
senses: The sense of ~mobil~ here is: the adjective ~mobil~ ("mobile, movable") as the resulting state.
The sense of ~mobil~ here is specifically military: to mobilize, to put on a war footing.

nach.chain: From MHG ~nāch~, from OHG ~nāh~ ("near, close"), from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhw~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~, generally connected to PIE *~h₂neḱ-~ ("to reach, attain"). The particle is the same word as the adjective ~nah~ ("near"). Cognate with English ~nigh~, whose old comparative and superlative survive as ~near~ and ~next~.
senses: The prefix conveys following after, pursuing something that has gone ahead.
The prefix conveys doing something afterwards, later than the main event.
The prefix conveys repetition or imitation — doing again what someone else did.
The prefix conveys checking or verifying by going back over something.
The prefix conveys yielding or slackening — giving way rather than holding firm.

nahe.chain: From MHG ~nāhe~, ~nāch~, from OHG ~nāh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhw~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~ ("near"), of uncertain further origin. Cognate with English ~nigh~, Dutch ~na~, Gothic ~nēƕ~. English preserves the whole old paradigm as three separate words: ~nigh~ is the positive, ~near~ the old comparative, and ~next~ the old superlative. In verbal compounds ~nahe-~ marks approach — ~nahebringen~, ~nahelegen~ ("to suggest," literally "to lay near").
senses: The sense of ~nahe~ here is: near, into close proximity.
The sense of ~nahe~ here is: figuratively, made accessible or intimate.
The sense of ~nahe~ here is: approaching, drawing close to someone or something.

nebeneinander.chain: Transparently ~neben~ ("beside") + ~einander~ ("one another"), hence "side by side." ~Neben~ is itself a fossil: OHG ~in eban~ ("on the same level") contracted through MHG ~eneben~ into a preposition, so it still contains ~eben~ ("level, even"). As a particle it says only that the action puts things alongside each other.
senses: The sense of ~nebeneinander-~ here is: "side by side, alongside one another".
The sense of ~nebeneinander-~ here is: of arranging or setting things in parallel.

neu.chain: From MHG ~niuwe~, from OHG ~niuwi~, from Proto-West Germanic *~niwi~, from Proto-Germanic *~niwjaz~, from PIE *~néwos~ ("new"). Cognate with English ~new~, Dutch ~nieuw~, Danish ~ny~, Latin ~novus~, Greek ~neos~, Sanskrit ~navas~.
senses: The sense of ~neu~ here is: the adjective ~neu~ ("new") as the resulting state.
The sense of ~neu~ here is: of doing something over again, afresh.

nieder.chain: Not a prefix but the adverb and adjective ~nieder~ ("low, down"), from MHG ~nider~, from OHG ~nidar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~niþer~, from Proto-Germanic *~niþer~, a comparative formation on PIE *~ni-~ ("down"). Cognate with English ~nether~, which survives chiefly in ~netherworld~ and in the name of the ~Netherlands~ — the low countries, ~die Niederlande~, the same compound word in both languages.
senses: The particle conveys downward motion — lowering or setting down.
The particle conveys forcing something down — striking, suppressing, or defeating it.
The particle is the elevated or literary counterpart of colloquial ~runter-~.

näher.chain: The comparative of ~nahe~ ("near"), from MHG ~næher~, from OHG ~nāhōr~. As a particle it means "closer, nearer," and the compounds it forms denote mostly figurative approach — ~näherbringen~ ("to bring closer, make accessible"), ~sich nähern~. English ~near~ is the same comparative, frozen: Old English ~nēar~ was the comparative of ~nēah~ ("nigh"), so English lost the positive and kept the comparative where German kept both.
senses: The sense of ~näher~ here is: closer, nearer, into greater proximity.
The sense of ~näher~ here is: figuratively, making something more accessible or better understood.
The sense of ~näher~ here is: approaching, drawing near to someone or something.

offen.chain: From MHG ~offen~, from OHG ~offan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~opan~, from Proto-Germanic *~upanaz~ — originally a past participle meaning "lifted up" and hence "uncovered, open," derived from *~upp~ ("up"), from PIE *~upo~ ("up, over"). Cognate with English ~open~, Dutch ~open~, Swedish ~öppen~. As a verbal particle it is resultative — ~offenlegen~ ("to disclose," literally "to lay open"), ~offenstehen~, ~offenbleiben~.
senses: The sense of ~offen~ here is: into an open or uncovered state.
The sense of ~offen~ here is: disclosed, laid bare, made public.
The sense of ~offen~ here is: left unsettled, not yet closed or decided.

platt.chain: Borrowed in the seventeenth century from Low German and Dutch ~plat~, itself from Old French ~plat~ ("flat"), from Vulgar Latin *~plattus~, from Greek ~platýs~ ("broad, flat"). English ~plate~ and ~platter~ come from the same French word, and ~place~ from the related Greek ~plateîa~ ("broad street"). The adjective also names a language: ~Plattdeutsch~ was the plain, level speech of the north as against elevated High German.
senses: The sense of ~platt~ here is: the adjective ~platt~ ("flat, flattened") as the resulting state.
The sense of ~platt~ here is colloquially, flattened in the figurative sense: dumbfounded.

preis.chain: The noun in an older sense, not the modern ~Preis~ ("price"). ~Preisgeben~ appears about 1600 meaning "to give up as booty, to abandon to seizure," and its ~preis~ is generally traced to Old French ~prise~ ("a taking, capture, prize"), the source of German ~Prise~ and of English ~prize~ in the naval sense of a captured ship. It was early conflated with the homophonous ~Preis~ ("praise, worth, price"), from MHG ~prīs~, from Old French ~pris~, from Latin ~pretium~ ("value, payment") — distinct words, and the verb preserves the first. Dutch ~prijsgeven~ is the same formation.
senses: The sense of ~preis~ here is: the older noun "booty, that which is surrendered" — to give up, abandon.
The sense of ~preis~ here is: to expose something, to lay it open to a force one cannot resist.
The sense of ~preis~ here is: of a secret, to divulge or betray it.

publik.chain: Borrowed from Latin ~pūblicus~ ("of the people, public"), formed to ~populus~ ("people") under the influence of ~pūbēs~ ("adult population"), and reinforced by French ~public~. In German it survives chiefly in particle constructions: to make, or to become, public knowledge. Cognate with English ~public~, ~publish~, ~republic~.
senses: The sense of ~publik~ here is: "public, publicly known" as the resulting state.
The sense of ~publik~ here is: of making something public, or of its becoming known.

quer.chain: From MHG ~twer~, ~dwer~ (also ~quer~), from OHG ~twerh~ ("oblique, transverse"), from Proto-West Germanic *~þwerh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þwerhaz~ ("crooked, athwart"); the initial ~tw-~ became ~qu-~ in Early New High German. Cognate with English ~thwart~ (which English took from Old Norse ~þvert~) and, probably, with ~queer~, borrowed from Low German — so ~quer~ and ~queer~ are doublets, both starting from "crosswise, off-kilter." In verbal compounds it means "across, athwart" — ~querschießen~, ~sich querstellen~ ("to obstruct").
senses: The sense of ~quer-~ here is: crosswise, transversely, at an angle to the expected direction.
The sense of ~quer-~ here is: obstructively, cutting across someone else's course.
The sense of ~quer-~ here is: across, from one side to the other.

ran.chain: A colloquial contraction of ~heran~ (~her-~ "toward the speaker" + ~an~ "at, on"), of the same everyday register as ~rauf~, ~raus~, ~rein~, ~rüber~. The deictic contrast is the useful fact: ~her-~ orients motion toward the speaker, ~hin-~ away from the speaker. As a particle it brings something up close.
senses: The sense of ~ran-~ here is: "up to, close up" — bringing something near.
The sense of ~ran-~ here is: colloquial for ~heran~; often exhortative, of getting down to a task.

rauf.chain: The colloquial contraction of ~herauf~ ("up, up toward the speaker"), itself ~her-~ + ~auf~. It belongs with ~raus~, ~rein~, ~runter~, ~rüber~ and ~ran~, all reduced from ~her-~ compounds. In speech the reduced form has largely displaced ~hinauf~ as well, so it no longer reliably carries ~her-~'s toward-the-speaker orientation.
senses: The sense of ~rauf-~ here is: directional, "up, upward".
The sense of ~rauf-~ here is: colloquially for either ~herauf~ or ~hinauf~, the deictic contrast neutralized.

raus.chain: A colloquial contraction of ~heraus~ ("out hither, out toward the speaker"), and in everyday speech of ~hinaus~ ("out thither") as well: the reduced form has lost the deictic contrast that the two full forms carry. Written standard German uses the unreduced ~heraus-~ or ~hinaus-~.
senses: ~raus-~ Marks outward motion, "out.".
Deictically neutral, unlike the full forms it replaces: it serves for motion both toward and away from the speaker.
Spoken and informal in register.

recht.chain: From MHG ~rëht~, from OHG ~rëht~, from Proto-West Germanic *~reht~ ("right, straight"), from Proto-Germanic *~rehtaz~, from PIE *~h₃reǵ-~ ("to straighten, direct"). Cognate with English ~right~, Dutch ~recht~, Latin ~rēctus~. The same root, through Latin ~regere~ and ~rēx~, gives English ~correct~, ~direct~ and ~regent~ — and, natively, German ~Reich~.
senses: The sense of ~recht-~ here is: "right, correct", as in conceding that someone is right.
The sense of ~recht-~ here is: predicatively with ~haben~ or ~geben~, "in the right".
The sense of ~recht-~ here is: adverbially, "properly, as it should be".

rein.chain: In these verbs this is not the adjective ~rein~ ("pure, clean") but the colloquial contraction of ~herein~, and often of ~hinein~ as well — that is, ~her~ or ~hin~ + ~ein~ ("in"). The two words are homographs with unrelated histories, and only the directional one forms these compounds.
senses: ~rein-~ means motion into something, the informal counterpart of ~herein-~ and ~hinein-~.
It belongs to spoken and informal register; written standard German prefers the full forms.
In some compounds it adds a sense of butting in — intruding into a conversation or an affair.

richtig.chain: The adjective ~richtig~ ("correct, proper"), from MHG ~rihtec~, formed with the suffix ~-ig~ on ~richten~ ("to set straight, direct, judge"), itself a causative built to ~recht~, from PIE *~h₃reǵ-~ ("to straighten, direct"). Its root relatives are English ~right~ and, through Latin ~regere~, ~correct~ and ~direct~. In separable compounds the adjective is resultative.
senses: The sense of ~richtig~ here is: as a resultative adjective, "into a correct state", as of setting a statement right.
The sense of ~richtig~ here is: predicatively, "correctly, rightly", of judging or of being in the right position.

rot.chain: From MHG ~rōt~, from OHG ~rōt~, from Proto-West Germanic *~raud~, from Proto-Germanic *~raudaz~, from PIE *~h₁rewdʰ-~ ("red"). Cognate with English ~red~, Dutch ~rood~, Danish ~rød~, Latin ~ruber~, Greek ~erythrós~, Sanskrit ~rudhira-~. It is among the most stable color words in Indo-European, recognizable in nearly every branch.
senses: The sense of ~rot~ here is: the adjective ~rot~ ("red") as the resulting state.
The sense of ~rot~ here is: of blushing, or of marking something in red.

rum.chain: A colloquial contraction of ~herum~ ("around, about"), itself ~her-~ + ~um~. The reduction is confined to speech and informal writing; the standard compound is ~herum-~.
senses: ~rum-~ Marks circular or aimless motion, "around, about.".
Often carries a dismissive tint of purposelessness (~rumsitzen~, ~rumlaufen~).
Spoken and informal in register.

rund.chain: Borrowed in MHG as ~runt~ from Old French ~ront~, ~roont~, from Latin ~rotundus~ ("round"), a derivative of ~rota~ ("wheel"). English ~round~ is the same borrowing made independently, and ~rotund~, ~rotate~, and ~roulette~ go back to ~rota~ as well; the inherited German word from that root is ~Rad~ ("wheel"), so the loan and the native word are distant relatives. As a particle it names roundness, or figuratively completeness, as the outcome.
senses: The sense of ~rund~ here is: the adjective ~rund~ ("round") as the resulting state.
The sense of ~rund~ here is: figuratively, of finishing or rounding something off.

runter.chain: A colloquial contraction of ~herunter~ ("down hither"), and in everyday speech of ~hinunter~ ("down thither") as well, so that the reduced form covers both directions the full forms distinguish. Written standard German uses ~herunter-~ or ~hinunter-~.
senses: ~runter-~ Marks downward motion, "down.".
Deictically neutral, unlike the full forms it replaces.
Spoken and informal in register.

rüber.chain: A colloquial contraction of ~herüber~ (~her-~ "toward the speaker" + ~über~ "over, across"), belonging with ~rauf~, ~raus~, ~rein~, ~ran~ in casual speech. It marks motion across to this side, the speaker's side.
senses: The sense of ~rüber-~ here is: "over, across to this side".
The sense of ~rüber-~ here is: colloquial for ~herüber~; informal register.

rück.chain: A bound combining form, never a free word. It is the older stem of ~Rücken~ ("back"), from OHG ~(h)ruggi~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), and it reaches verbs by way of ~zurück~ — OHG ~zi rugge~, "toward the back." Compounds keep the short form (~rückerstatten~, ~rückfragen~, ~Rückkehr~) where a finite verb would take the full adverb ~zurück~. English ~ridge~ is the same Proto-Germanic word: Old English ~hrycg~ meant both a person's back and the spine of a hill.
senses: The sense of ~rück-~ here is: back, backwards, in the reverse direction.
The sense of ~rück-~ here is: returning something to its origin or to an earlier state.
The sense of ~rück-~ here is: in response, referring back to something already said.

rückwärts.chain: From ~Rücken~ ("back") plus the adverbial suffix ~-wärts~, from OHG ~-wert~, from Proto-Germanic *~werþaz~ ("turned toward"), from PIE *~wert-~ ("to turn") — exactly the English ~-ward~ of ~backward~ and ~homeward~. ~Rücken~ itself goes back to OHG ~(h)rukki~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~, whose English descendant is ~ridge~, the back or spine of a hill. As a particle it orients the action backward.
senses: The sense of ~rückwärts-~ here is: "backward, in reverse".
The sense of ~rückwärts-~ here is: of reversing an action or running it in the opposite direction.

satt.chain: From MHG ~sat~, from OHG ~sat~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sad~, from Proto-Germanic *~sadaz~, from PIE *~seh₂-~ ("to satiate"). Cognate with Dutch ~zat~, Danish ~sat~, and English ~sad~, which in Old English meant "sated, weary" long before it meant "sorrowful"; the same root gives Latin ~satis~ ("enough"), whence English ~satisfy~ and ~saturate~. In separable compounds the adjective is resultative: the verb continues until the subject has had its fill.
senses: The sense of ~satt~ here is: as a resultative adjective, "to satiety, until full".
The sense of ~satt~ here is: reflexively, "until one has had enough" of seeing, hearing or eating something.
The sense of ~satt~ here is: with ~haben~, "to be fed up with".

sauber.chain: The adjective ~sauber~ ("clean"), from MHG ~sūber~, from OHG ~sūbar~, borrowed from Latin ~sōbrius~ ("sober, temperate, level-headed"), itself from ~sē-~ ("without") + ~ēbrius~ ("drunk"). The sense drifted from "temperate" through "unblemished" to "clean". Cognate with Dutch ~zuiver~ and, by a different route out of the same Latin word, English ~sober~. In a resultative compound the adjective names the end state: to verb something until it is clean.
senses: The sense of ~sauber~ here is: clean — the state a thing is brought into.
The sense of ~sauber~ here is: tidily, without mess.
The sense of ~sauber~ here is in ~saubermachen~: to clean up.

scheckig.chain: The adjective ~scheckig~ ("blotchy, piebald"), from MHG ~scheckeht~, to MHG ~schecke~, borrowed from Old French ~eschec~, plural ~eschès~ ("chess; chessboard") — a pattern named for the board. The noun ~Schecke~ ("piebald horse") was back-formed from the adjective in the 16th century. English ~check~, ~checkered~, ~chess~, and ~exchequer~ all descend from that same Old French word, which goes back through Arabic to Persian ~šāh~ ("king"), so a mottled German horse and the British Exchequer are named from the same chessboard.
senses: The sense of ~scheckig~ here is: blotchy, mottled, piebald — the state reached.
The sense of ~scheckig~ here is in ~sich scheckig lachen~: to the point of helpless laughter.

schief.chain: The adjective ~schief~ ("crooked, askew"), from northern MHG ~schief~/~schīf~, taken from Middle Low German ~schēf~, from Old Saxon *~skēf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skaib~, from Proto-Germanic *~skaibaz~. Cognate with Dutch ~scheef~, Swedish ~skev~, and Old Norse ~skeifr~; English ~skew~ resembles it but reached English through Old Northern French and is not securely the same word. In verbs it is resultative and figurative — ~schiefgehen~ is for a plan to come out crooked, that is, to go wrong.
senses: The sense of ~schief~ here is resultative: leaves the object crooked or at a slant.
The sense of ~schief~ here is: figuratively, turning out wrong or badly.

schlapp.chain: A Low German form, from Middle Low German ~slap~ ("limp, flaccid"), a doublet of High German ~schlaff~; both go back to Proto-Germanic *~slap-~ and are usually traced to PIE *~(s)leh₂b-~ ("to be weak, limp"), the root also behind ~schlafen~ and Latin ~labāre~ ("to totter"). Cognate with Dutch ~slap~. The Low German ~p~ against High German ~ff~ is the giveaway that the word travelled north to south rather than passing through the High German consonant shift.
senses: The sense of ~schlapp~ here is: as a resultative adjective, "limp, exhausted".
The sense of ~schlapp~ here is: of a person giving out, "to the point of collapse from exhaustion".

schlecht.chain: From MHG ~slëht~, from OHG ~slëht~ ("straight, level, plain"), from Proto-Germanic *~slihtaz~ ("smooth, level"); the origin beyond Germanic is uncertain. Cognate with English ~slight~, Dutch ~slecht~, Swedish ~slät~, Icelandic ~sléttur~. ~schlecht~ and ~schlicht~ are one word split in two: "plain, simple" stayed with ~schlicht~ while ~schlecht~ slid from "plain" to "inferior" to "bad" — much the slide English ~slight~ made from "smooth" to "trifling".
senses: The sense of ~schlecht~ here is as a resultative adjective, "badly": the verb makes its object bad or worse.
The sense of ~schlecht~ here is: of speech, "disparagingly", as in running someone down.

schwarz.chain: From MHG ~swarz~, from OHG ~swarz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~swart~, from Proto-Germanic *~swartaz~ ("black, dark"), from PIE *~swordos~ ("dirty, dark"). Cognate with English ~swarthy~, Old English ~sweart~, Dutch ~zwart~, Swedish ~svart~; Latin ~sordēs~ ("filth," whence English ~sordid~) belongs to the same root. As a verbal particle it is either resultative or figurative — ~schwarzfahren~ ("to ride without a ticket") and ~schwarzarbeiten~ use ~schwarz~ in its later sense "illicit, off the books."
senses: The sense of ~schwarz~ here is: into a black or blackened state.
The sense of ~schwarz~ here is: illicitly, without authorization, off the books.
The sense of ~schwarz~ here is: figuratively, in a dark or pessimistic manner.

schön.chain: The adjective ~schön~ ("beautiful"), from MHG ~schœne~, from OHG ~scōni~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skaunī~, from Proto-Germanic *~skauniz~, built on the root of ~schauen~ ("to look") and so originally "worth beholding." Cognate with English ~sheen~, once meaning "beautiful, bright." As a particle it is resultative and usually ironic: ~schönreden~ and ~schönfärben~ make something look good rather than be good.
senses: The sense of ~schön~ here is resultative: makes the object beautiful or presentable.
~schön~, ironically, makes something merely appear better than it is.
The sense of ~schön~ here is: often carries a note of glossing over or whitewashing.

seil.chain: The noun ~Seil~ ("rope, cord"), from MHG ~seil~, from OHG ~seil~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sail~, from Proto-Germanic *~sailą~, probably from PIE *~seh₁i-~ ("to bind, tie"). Cognate with Dutch ~zeel~, Old English ~sāl~ ("rope, cord"), Old Norse ~seil~; German ~Saite~, the string of an instrument, comes from the same root. The noun is incorporated as the instrument of the action: ~seilspringen~ is to skip rope.
senses: The sense of ~seil~ here is: the rope, incorporated as the instrument of the action.
The sense of ~seil~ here is in ~seilspringen~: to skip rope, to jump rope.

selig.chain: From MHG ~sælec~, from OHG ~sālīg~ ("blessed, happy"), from Proto-West Germanic *~sālīg~, a ~-g~ derivative of *~sāli~ ("good fortune"). Cognate with Dutch ~zalig~, Swedish ~salig~, and Old English ~sǣliġ~ — which is modern English ~silly~, by way of "blessed" to "innocent" to "simple" to "foolish", one of the steeper semantic falls in English. In compounds the adjective is resultative, chiefly in the church's ~seligsprechen~, literally "to pronounce blessed".
senses: The sense of ~selig~ here is: as a resultative adjective, "blessed", of declaring someone so.
The sense of ~selig~ here is: ecclesiastically, of beatification, the step below canonization.

sicher.chain: The adjective ~sicher~ ("safe, certain"), from MHG ~sicher~, ~siher~, from OHG ~sihhur~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sikur~, borrowed from Latin ~sēcūrus~ ("free from care, safe"), from ~sē-~ ("without") + ~cūra~ ("care"). English ~secure~ (straight from Latin) and ~sure~ (through Old French) are the same word arriving twice. As a particle it names the end state: ~sicherstellen~ is to put a thing beyond doubt, ~sichergehen~ to make certain of it.
senses: The sense of ~sicher~ here is: safe, secure — the state something is brought into.
The sense of ~sicher~ here is: certain, beyond doubt.
The sense of ~sicher~ here is in ~sichergehen~: to make sure, to play it safe.

sonder.chain: From MHG ~sunder~, from OHG ~suntar~ ("apart, separately; without"), from Proto-Germanic *~sundraz~, from PIE *~sn̥ter-~ ("apart, for oneself"). As a preposition meaning "without" it is archaic, surviving only in frozen phrases such as ~sonder Tadel~; as a bound first element meaning "separate, special" it remains fully productive (~Sonderzug~, ~Sonderfall~, ~sonderkündigen~). Cognate with English ~sunder~, ~asunder~, and ~sundry~, and beyond Germanic with Latin ~sine~ ("without") and Ancient Greek ~áter~.
senses: The sense of ~sonder-~ here is: special, extraordinary — outside the ordinary case.
The sense of ~sonder-~ here is: separate, set apart from the rest.
The sense of ~sonder-~ here is archaic prepositional sense: without.

stand.chain: The noun ~Stand~ ("standing, position, footing"), a verbal noun to ~stehen~, from MHG ~stant~, ultimately from PIE *~steh₂-~ ("to stand"). In ~standhalten~ it is incorporated as the object: literally "to hold one's stand", hence to hold one's ground, to withstand. Cognate with English ~stand~ as a noun, and belonging to the same root as ~Statt~, ~Stätte~, and ~Stadt~.
senses: The sense of ~stand~ here is: one's standing or footing, incorporated as the object.
The sense of ~stand~ here is in ~standhalten~: to hold one's ground, to withstand.

stark.chain: The adjective ~stark~ ("strong"), from MHG ~starc~, from OHG ~starc~, ~starah~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stark~, from Proto-Germanic *~starkaz~ ("stiff, rigid"), from PIE *~ster-~ ("stiff"). Cognate with English ~stark~, which kept the older "rigid, utter" sense, as well as Dutch ~sterk~ and Swedish ~stark~. The resultative frame gives "to make strong": ~sich für etwas starkmachen~ is to throw one's weight behind a cause.
senses: The sense of ~stark~ here is: strong — the state something is brought into.
The sense of ~stark~ here is in ~sich starkmachen für~: to stand up for, to campaign for.

statt.chain: The noun ~Statt~ ("place, stead"), from MHG ~stat~, from OHG ~stat~, from Proto-Germanic *~stadiz~, from PIE *~steh₂-~ ("to stand") — not the preposition ~statt~ ("instead of"), which is a later reduction of ~anstatt~, itself built on this same noun. ~Statt~, ~Stadt~ and ~Stätte~ are one Old High German word split three ways; the bare noun now survives mainly in fixed phrases such as ~an meiner Statt~. Cognate with English ~stead~ (as in ~instead~, ~homestead~) and Dutch ~stad~.
senses: The sense of ~statt~ here is the incorporated noun "place" as the verb's object: ~stattfinden~ is literally "to find place", exactly the idiom behind English ~take place~.
The sense of ~statt~ here is: "place, room" in the sense of yielding it, i.e. granting a request or upholding an appeal.

stecken.chain: The verb ~stecken~ ("to be stuck, to be lodged in place"), from MHG ~stecken~, from OHG ~steckōn~, a geminate derivative of OHG ~stehhan~ (whence ~stechen~, "to prick, stab"), from Proto-Germanic *~stikaną~, from PIE *~(s)teyg-~ ("to be sharp, to stab"). The sense runs from a pointed thing driven into a surface to a thing simply fixed there. Cognate with English ~stick~ and ~steak~, the latter originally meat on a stick. As a particle it names the state the subject remains in: ~steckenbleiben~ is to get stuck and stay stuck.
senses: The sense of ~stecken~ here is: stuck, lodged, immobile — the state the subject remains in.
The sense of ~stecken~ here is in ~steckenbleiben~: to get stuck, to break down or falter mid-way.

stehen.chain: The verb ~stehen~ ("to stand"), from MHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from OHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stān~, from Proto-Germanic *~stāną~, from PIE *~steh₂-~ ("to stand"). Cognate with English ~stand~, Dutch ~staan~, and Latin ~stāre~. As a particle it names the state the subject or object remains in: ~stehenbleiben~ is to stop and stay standing, ~stehenlassen~ to leave a thing where it stands.
senses: The sense of ~stehen~ here is: standing, in place — the state the subject or object remains in.
The sense of ~stehen~ here is in ~stehenbleiben~: to come to a halt, to stop, to stay put.
The sense of ~stehen~ here is in ~stehenlassen~: to leave something where it is.

still.chain: From MHG ~stille~, from OHG ~stilli~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stillī~, from Proto-Germanic *~stillijaz~ ("still, motionless"), from PIE *~stel-~ ("to place, set") — the sense runs from "set in place" to "not moving" to "silent." Cognate with English ~still~, Dutch ~stil~, Low German ~still~; the same PIE root gave ~stellen~ and English ~stall~. As a verbal particle it is resultative — ~stillstehen~, ~stilllegen~ ("to shut down"), ~stillhalten~.
senses: The sense of ~still~ here is: into a state of stillness or silence.
The sense of ~still~ here is: brought to a halt, shut down.
The sense of ~still~ here is: quietly, without disturbance or protest.

stramm.chain: The adjective ~stramm~ ("taut, tight, rigid"), from Middle Low German ~stram~, spreading into standard German from the north; the further origin is uncertain, and the word may be expressive in nature. Cognate with Dutch ~stram~ ("stiff"), itself probably a Low German loan. In ~strammstehen~, "to stand at attention", the adjective describes the posture the subject holds — drawn up, rigid, taut.
senses: The sense of ~stramm~ here is: taut, tight, rigid — the posture or state held.
The sense of ~stramm~ here is in ~strammstehen~: to stand at attention.

stumm.chain: The adjective ~stumm~ ("mute"), from MHG and OHG ~stum~, from a Proto-Germanic base *~stumm-~, from PIE *~stem-~ ("to push, to halt, to stutter") — the original sense is "hindered in speech". It stands in ablaut relation to ~stammeln~ and ~stemmen~, and is cognate with Dutch ~stom~ and English ~stammer~. The resultative frame yields the modern coinage ~stummschalten~, "to switch to mute".
senses: The sense of ~stumm~ here is: mute, silent — the state something is put into.
The sense of ~stumm~ here is in ~stummschalten~: to mute a device or a microphone.

teil.chain: The noun ~Teil~ ("part, share"), from MHG ~teil~, from OHG ~teil~, from Proto-West Germanic *~daili~, from Proto-Germanic *~dailiz~, tentatively from PIE *~dʰeh₁-~ ("to put, set") by way of a stem meaning "portion". Cognate with English ~deal~ (as in "a great deal", a portion) and ~dole~, and with Dutch ~deel~. The noun is incorporated as the object, and the construction calques Latin ~participāre~: Dutch ~deelnemen~ and English ~take part~ render the same model with native material. Being grammaticalized, it is written lowercase when separated — ~ich nehme teil~.
senses: The sense of ~teil~ here is: a part or share, incorporated as the object of the verb.
The sense of ~teil~ here is in ~teilnehmen~: to take part, to participate, to attend.
The sense of ~teil~ here is in ~teilhaben~: to have a share in something.

tot.chain: From the adjective ~tot~ ("dead"), from MHG ~tōt~, from OHG ~tōt~, from Proto-West Germanic *~daud~, from Proto-Germanic *~daudaz~, a participial formation to *~dawjaną~ ("to die"), from PIE *~dʰew-~ ("to pass away, die"). Cognate with English ~dead~, Dutch ~dood~, Swedish ~död~.
senses: In a resultative compound ~tot-~ names the end state: the action is carried on until the object is dead — ~totschlagen~ is to beat someone to death.
It is very often hyperbolic rather than literal, as of laughing or working oneself to death.
The sense of ~tot~ here is: Applied to things it means "deadened, silenced, put out of use.".

um.chain: From MHG ~umbe~, from OHG ~umbi~, from Proto-West Germanic *~umbi~, from Proto-Germanic *~umbi~ ("around"), from PIE *~h₂m̥bʰi~ ("around, on either side of"). ~Um-~ is one of German's separability doublets: stressed and separable it is literal and spatial (~úmfahren~, "to run over"), unstressed and inseparable it is figurative (~umfáhren~, "to drive around"); the senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with Latin ~ambi-~ (in ~ambiguous~, literally "driving both ways") and Greek ~amphí-~ (in ~amphitheater~, a theater with seats all around).
senses: As a separable prefix, it conveys motion around something, circling or circulating.
As a separable prefix, it conveys toppling — falling or knocking over.
As a separable prefix, it conveys change or conversion — doing something over differently.
As a separable prefix, it conveys repositioning — moving something from one place to another.

umeinander.chain: Transparently ~um~ ("around") + ~einander~ ("one another"), a reciprocal compound adverb of the same shape as ~auseinander~, ~durcheinander~, and ~nebeneinander~. It contributes exactly what its parts say: the participants are arranged around, or concerned with, one another. See the entries for ~um~ and for the ~einander~ adverbs.
senses: The sense of ~umeinander-~ here is: around one another, in a ring.
The sense of ~umeinander-~ here is: with respect to one another, reciprocally.

umher.chain: The preposition ~um~ ("around") compounded with the deictic adverb ~her~ ("hither"): motion in a circuit, and by extension in no particular direction at all. Transparently compositional; the etymology belongs to the two component entries.
senses: The sense of ~umher-~ here is: directional, "around, about, in all directions".
The sense of ~umher-~ here is: with verbs of motion, an aimless or wandering manner.

unter.chain: From MHG ~under~, from OHG ~untar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~under~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~ ("under, between, among"), from PIE *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"). Cognate with English ~under~, Dutch ~onder~, Sanskrit ~adhás~ ("below"). Proto-Germanic *~under~ appears to have absorbed a second, distinct etymon meaning "between" (the source of Latin ~inter~), which is why the particle still carries both senses.
senses: Stressed and separable, ~unter-~ is literal and spatial: something goes, is placed, or is written underneath.
It also means "among, in the middle of," as of mixing one thing in with others.
With verbs of housing it means bringing someone under a roof — into shelter or accommodation.
The unstressed inseparable ~unter-~ is a different creature, taking abstract senses of support, subjection, and interruption.

verloren.chain: The past participle of ~verlieren~ ("to lose"), used predicatively: ~verlorengehen~ is literally "to go lost", the German counterpart of English ~get lost~ and ~go missing~. ~Verlieren~ is from MHG ~verliesen~, from OHG ~firliosan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fraleusaną~, from PIE *~lewH-~ ("to cut off, to loosen"); the ~-r-~ of the modern infinitive was levelled in from the participle, so ~verloren~ preserves the older shape of the two. English keeps the very same participle in ~forlorn~ and ~lovelorn~.
senses: The sense of ~verloren~ here is: lost, gone — the state the subject passes into.
The sense of ~verloren~ here is in ~verlorengehen~: to get lost, to go missing, to be wasted.

voll.chain: From MHG ~vol~, from OHG ~fol~, from Proto-West Germanic *~foll~, from Proto-Germanic *~fullaz~ ("full"), from PIE *~pleh₁-~ ("to fill"). Cognate with English ~full~, Dutch ~vol~, Gothic ~fulls~; Latin ~plēnus~ ("full") is from the same root, whence English ~plenty~ and ~replenish~. The separable particle ~voll-~ is resultative (~vollmachen~, ~volltanken~), and it should not be confused with the homophonous inseparable ~voll-~ of ~vollenden~ and ~vollbringen~, which means "completely" and never separates.
senses: The sense of ~voll~ here is: completely full, filled to capacity.
The sense of ~voll~ here is: fully, to the full extent.
The sense of ~voll~ here is: filling something up as the result of the action.

vonstatten.chain: A fossilized prepositional phrase, ~von~ + ~statten~, in which ~statten~ is the old dative plural of MHG ~state~ ("place, opportunity, favourable position") — the same noun as ~Statt~ and ~Stätte~, ultimately from PIE *~steh₂-~ ("to stand"). It survives only in ~vonstattengehen~, "to proceed, to come off", beside the parallel fossil ~zustattenkommen~ ("to come in useful"). English keeps that noun alive in ~stead~ and ~instead~.
senses: The sense of ~vonstatten-~ here is: from its place, forward — a fossilized dative-plural phrase.
The sense of ~vonstatten-~ here is in ~vonstattengehen~: to proceed, to go off, to take place.

vor.chain: From MHG ~vor~, ~vore~, from OHG ~fora~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fura~, from Proto-Germanic *~furai~, from PIE *~pr̥h₂-éy~, a case form of the root *~preh₂-~ ("before, in front"). Cognate with English ~fore~ and ~before~, Dutch ~voor~, Gothic ~faura~, and, from the same root, Latin ~prae~ and ~prō~.
senses: The prefix conveys forward motion or position in front.
The prefix conveys doing something in advance, before the need arises.
The prefix conveys presenting or performing something for an audience.
The prefix conveys precedence — putting one thing ahead of another.

voran.chain: A transparent compound of ~vor~ ("before, in front," from OHG ~fora~, from PIE *~per-~) and ~an~ ("on, at"), together "out in front and pressing on," hence "ahead, forward, onward." It differs from bare ~vor-~ in adding the sense of continued progress.
senses: Marks position at the head of something, going first (~vorangehen~).
Marks progress, the thing advancing rather than merely being in front (~vorankommen~, ~vorantreiben~).

voraus.chain: The compound adverb ~vor~ ("before, in front of") + ~aus~ ("out"); see those entries for their separate histories. Together they mean "ahead, in advance."
senses: ~voraus-~ means going on ahead of others in space.
More often it is temporal: doing something in advance, before the fact.
The sense of ~voraus-~ here is: In ~vorausgesetzt~ it has hardened into a fixed sense, "presupposed, granted that.".

vorbei.chain: A transparent compound of ~vor~ ("before, in front") and ~bei~ ("by, near"): something passes in front of and close by, hence "past, by." Like ~dahin~ it took on a temporal sense — ~vorbei~ alone means "over, finished."
senses: Marks motion past something without stopping.
Of a brief visit, dropping by (~vorbeikommen~, ~vorbeischauen~).
Of missing a target, going past rather than into it (~vorbeischießen~, ~vorbeireden~).

vorher.chain: Transparently ~vor~ ("before") + ~her~, the deictic adverb of motion toward the speaker and, temporally, from an earlier point. The compound means "beforehand, in advance," and in verbal compounds it places an action prior to some reference point — ~vorhersagen~ ("to predict"), ~vorhersehen~ ("to foresee"). See the entries for ~vor-~ and ~her-~ for the component histories.
senses: The sense of ~vorher-~ here is: beforehand, in advance, ahead of time.
The sense of ~vorher-~ here is: prior to some reference point in the sequence of events.
The sense of ~vorher-~ here is: anticipating what is still to come.

vorlieb.chain: A univerbation of the preposition ~vor~ (beside the variant ~für~) with ~lieb~ in the accusative neuter, attested from the 16th century: ~vorlieb nehmen~ is "to take [a thing] for agreeable", hence to make do with it. ~Lieb~ is the ordinary adjective "dear, agreeable", cognate with English ~lief~ (as in ~I would as lief~) and with ~love~. The phrase has frozen solid: ~vorlieb~ occurs nowhere else, and the older variant ~fürliebnehmen~ is now archaic.
senses: The sense of ~vorlieb-~ here is: for [something] agreeable — a frozen prepositional phrase.
The sense of ~vorlieb-~ here is in ~vorliebnehmen~: to make do with, to settle for, to content oneself with.

vorweg.chain: The adverb ~vorweg~, ~vor~ ("before, in front") + ~weg~ ("away"), literally "forward away", hence "ahead, in advance, beforehand". It is transparently compositional; see the entries for ~vor~ and ~weg~. ~Vorwegnehmen~ is to take a thing in advance — to anticipate it, or to give away an ending.
senses: The sense of ~vorweg-~ here is: in advance, beforehand, ahead of the rest.
The sense of ~vorweg-~ here is in ~vorwegnehmen~: to anticipate, to pre-empt, to give away.

vorüber.chain: The adverb ~vor~ ("before, in front") compounded with ~über~ ("over, across"): past a point and beyond it. Transparently compositional and close in sense to ~vorbei~; the etymology belongs to the two component entries.
senses: The sense of ~vorüber-~ here is: directional, "past, by", of moving alongside something and on beyond it.
The sense of ~vorüber-~ here is: temporally, "over, at an end".

wach.chain: The adjective ~wach~ ("awake") is young: a sixteenth-century back-formation from the noun ~Wache~ ("watch, guard"), taking the place of older ~wacker~. Its family is ~wachen~, from OHG ~wahhēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~wakāną~, from PIE *~weǵ-~ ("to be lively, vigorous"). Cognate with Old English ~wacian~ (English ~wake~), Dutch ~waken~, Old Norse ~vaka~, Gothic ~gawaknan~; through Latin ~vigil~ and ~vigēre~ the same root gives English ~vigil~ and ~vigour~.
senses: The sense of ~wach~ here is as a resultative adjective, "awake": the verb brings someone into wakefulness.
The sense of ~wach~ here is: figuratively, "alert, alive", of keeping a memory or an issue current.

wahr.chain: Two different words fall together in this spelling. In ~wahrsagen~ it is the adjective ~wahr~ ("true"), from MHG ~wār~, from OHG ~wār~, from Proto-Germanic *~wēraz~, from PIE *~weh₁ro-~ ("true, trustworthy"), cognate with Latin ~vērus~ (whence English ~very~, ~verify~, ~verdict~) and Old Irish ~fír~. In ~wahrnehmen~ it is instead the old feminine noun OHG ~wara~, MHG ~war(e)~ ("attention, heed, watchfulness"), from PIE *~wer-~ ("to watch out for, to perceive"): OHG ~wara neman~ was "to take heed", and only in Middle High German did it narrow to sensory perception. That second root is the one English keeps in ~aware~, ~beware~, and ~wary~, so ~wahrnehmen~ is a closer relative of ~be aware~ than of ~true~.
senses: The sense of ~wahr-~ here is: heed, attention — the old noun ~wara~, incorporated as the object.
The sense of ~wahr-~ here is in ~wahrnehmen~: to perceive, to notice, to exercise (a right, an office).
The sense of ~wahr-~ here is in ~wahrsagen~: the adjective ~wahr~ — to speak true, to prophesy.

warm.chain: From the adjective ~warm~, from MHG ~warm~, from OHG ~warm~, from Proto-West Germanic *~warm~, from Proto-Germanic *~warmaz~, of uncertain further origin: either PIE *~wer-~ ("to burn") or PIE *~gʷʰer-~ ("warm, hot"), the latter of which would make it a distant relative of Ancient Greek ~thermós~ and Latin ~formus~. Cognate with English ~warm~, Dutch ~warm~, Swedish ~varm~. As a separable particle it is resultative: the verb brings its object into a warm state.
senses: The sense of ~warm~ here is resultative: the action brings something to a warm state.
The sense of ~warm~ here is: of engines, muscles, or a performer, bringing up to working temperature.
The sense of ~warm~ here is: figuratively, thawing a cold relation or keeping something hospitable.

weg.chain: Not a prefix but the adverb ~weg~ ("away"), shortened from MHG ~enwec~, from OHG ~in weg~ ("on the way"); the noun ~Weg~ descends from Proto-Germanic *~wegaz~, from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to go, to transport"), the root behind Latin ~vehere~ and English ~wagon~ and ~vehicle~. English built its equivalent from exactly the same parts: ~away~ is Old English ~onweg~, also literally "on the way." The adverb has since shortened its vowel, which is all that now distinguishes it from the noun ~Weg~.
senses: The particle conveys departure or removal from a place — going or taking away.
The particle conveys disposal — getting rid of something for good.

weich.chain: From the adjective ~weich~ ("soft"), from MHG ~weich~, from OHG ~weih~, from Proto-West Germanic *~waik~, from Proto-Germanic *~waikwaz~, a derivative of *~wīkaną~ ("to yield, to give way") — softness understood as the property of giving way, which is still the sense of ~weichen~. Cognate with Dutch ~week~, Old English ~wāc~, and Old Norse ~veikr~; English borrowed the Norse form as ~weak~ after its own ~wāc~ died out, so ~weich~ and ~weak~ are the same word by two routes. As a particle it is resultative: the verb softens its object.
senses: The sense of ~weich~ here is resultative: the action renders something soft.
The sense of ~weich~ here is: of cooking, boiling or simmering until tender.
The sense of ~weich~ here is: of beating or working a material until it yields.

weis.chain: Neither ~weiß~ ("white") nor ~weise~ in its modern sense, but the older adjective ~weis~ ("knowing, informed"), from MHG ~wīs~, from OHG ~wīs~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wīs~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīsaz~, from PIE *~weyd-~ ("to see, to know") — the root of ~wissen~ and ~weisen~, of Latin ~vidēre~, and of English ~wise~, ~wit~, and ~wisdom~. MHG ~wīs machen~ meant "to make someone knowledgeable, to instruct", a sense that held into the eighteenth century; in the sixteenth it acquired the ironic reading "to make someone believe something untrue", which has since driven the honest one out. The particle now survives essentially only in ~weismachen~, a fossil of the older sense.
senses: ~weis-~ makes someone "knowing" of something — in modern use, of something false.
~weis-~ carries the ironic sense of fobbing a story off on a credulous hearer.

weiter.chain: The comparative of the adjective ~weit~ ("wide, far"), hence "further, onward." ~Weit~ comes from MHG ~wīt~, from OHG ~wīt~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wīd~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīdaz~ ("wide"), most likely from PIE *~wi-itós~ ("gone apart"), from *~wi-~ ("apart, in two") + *~h₁ey-~ ("to go"). Cognate with English ~wide~, Dutch ~wijd~, Swedish ~vid~.
senses: As a separable particle ~weiter-~ means "further, onward," marking the continuation of an action already under way.
With verbs of transfer it means "on to the next person," as in passing something along.
It can also mark plain spatial advance: moving further in a direction already taken.

wert.chain: From the adjective ~wert~ ("worthy, worth"), from MHG ~wert~, from OHG ~werd~, from Proto-West Germanic *~werþ~, from Proto-Germanic *~werþaz~; the PIE source is uncertain, possibly *~wert-~ ("to turn"). Cognate with English ~worth~, Dutch ~waard~, Swedish ~värd~, and the source of the noun ~Wert~ ("value"). As a particle it is evaluative: the verb treats its object as having worth.
senses: ~wert~ marks the object as esteemed or held in value.
The sense of ~wert~ here is resultative: the action assigns or acknowledges worth.

wett.chain: From the adjective ~wett~ ("even, quits, square"), which is the MHG noun ~wette~ ("payment of a debt, compensation") frozen into a predicate: around 1300 ~wette werden~ meant "to be settled", hence "free of debt", hence "even", and the ending was gone by the seventeenth century. The noun survives as ~Wette~ ("wager") and ~wetten~ ("to bet"), from Proto-Germanic *~wadją~ ("pledge"), cognate with English ~wed~ — a wedding being, etymologically, a pledge, and English ~wage~ and ~wager~ the same word again by way of Frankish and French. The particle keeps the accounting metaphor: the verb balances the books.
senses: ~wett~ marks a settling of accounts: making good a debt, loss, or fault.
The sense of ~wett~ here is: offsetting something negative with something positive.

wichtig.chain: From the adjective ~wichtig~, borrowed in the sixteenth century from Middle Low German ~wichtich~ ("weighty, heavy"), a merchants' word built on ~wicht~ ("weight", modern ~Gewicht~) that spread from the northern trading cities southward. That noun belongs with ~wiegen~ and ~wägen~, from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to move, to convey"), the root behind English ~weigh~, ~wagon~, and ~way~ and Latin ~vehere~. The metaphor is still live and matches English exactly: what matters is what weighs, as in ~weighty~.
senses: ~wichtig~ marks importance, chiefly in ~wichtigtun~, to act important.
The sense of ~wichtig~ here is: with a note of self-importance or puffery.

wider.chain: From MHG ~wider~, from OHG ~widar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wiþr~, from Proto-Germanic *~wiþrą~ ("against, back"), from PIE *~wi-tero-~ ("further apart"), a comparative of *~wi-~ ("apart, in two"). Cognate with Dutch ~weder~, Old Norse ~viðr~, and English ~with~, whose original sense was "against" and survives in ~withstand~ and ~withhold~. Three things must be kept apart: separable stressed ~wider-~ (~widerhallen~, ~widerspiegeln~), which means "back"; inseparable unstressed ~wider-~ (~widersprechen~, ~widerstehen~), which means "against"; and ~wieder~ ("again"), which is the very same word, split off from ~wider~ by a purely orthographic convention that grammarians did not settle until the eighteenth century.
senses: The sense of ~wider-~ here is separable and stressed, the particle means "back": the action is returned or thrown back.
The sense of ~wider-~ here is: in verbs of reflection and echo, the image or sound is cast back.
The sense of ~wider-~ here is: distinct from unstressed inseparable ~wider-~ ("against") and from the homophone ~wieder~ ("again").

wieder.chain: From MHG ~wider~, from OHG ~widar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wiþr~, from Proto-Germanic *~wiþra~ ("against, back"), from PIE *~wi-tero-~ ("more apart"), a comparative of *~wi-~ ("apart, in two"). Cognate with English ~with~, which originally meant "against" — a sense English still preserves in ~withstand~ and ~withhold~. German keeps the two developments apart in spelling: ~wieder~ "again" beside ~wider~ "against."
senses: As a separable particle ~wieder-~ means "again": the action is repeated.
It also means "back," of returning something to its origin or to an earlier state.
A few compounds are inseparable and mean pure repetition, as in ~wiederholen~ ("to repeat"), where the stress falls on ~-ho-~ rather than on the particle.

wiederauf.chain: A stacked particle: ~wieder~ ("again") + ~auf~ ("up"), as in ~wiederaufbauen~ ("to rebuild"). ~wieder~ is etymologically the same word as ~wider~ ("against"), separated from it only by spelling convention; ~auf~ goes back to Proto-Germanic *~upp~, cognate with English ~up~. See the ~wieder~ and ~auf~ entries for the components.
senses: The sense of ~wiederauf-~ here is repetition of an ~auf-~ action: doing again what has been undone.
The sense of ~wiederauf-~ here is: chiefly reconstruction and resumption — rebuilding, taking up, or starting anew.

wohl.chain: From the adverb ~wohl~ ("well"), from MHG ~wol~, ~wole~, from OHG ~wola~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wela~, from Proto-Germanic *~wela~, from PIE *~welh₁-~ ("to wish, to choose"). That is the same root as ~wollen~ ("to want") and Latin ~velle~: to be ~wohl~ is, etymologically, to be as one would wish. Cognate with English ~well~, Dutch ~wel~, Swedish ~väl~, Danish ~vel~, and the source of the noun ~Wohl~ ("welfare").
senses: ~wohl-~ marks the action as done well, kindly, or to good effect.
~wohl-~, with reflexives, marks a state of comfort or ease.
The sense of ~wohl-~ here is: in older or elevated compounds, a formulaic note of benevolence.

wund.chain: From MHG ~wunt~, from OHG ~wunt~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wund~, from Proto-Germanic *~wundaz~ ("wounded"), beside the verb *~wundōną~ ("to wound"); the origin beyond Germanic is uncertain. Cognate with English ~wound~, Dutch ~wond~, Gothic ~wunds~. As a separable element it is resultative and almost always reflexive: the action is carried on until the body is raw from it.
senses: The sense of ~wund~ here is: as a resultative adjective, "sore, chafed", from repeated action.
The sense of ~wund~ here is: reflexively, of rubbing, walking or lying until the skin is raw.

zu.chain: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~.
senses: The prefix conveys direction toward a goal or target.
The prefix means "shut" — closing something.
The prefix conveys addition or increase — adding to what is already there.
The prefix conveys allocation — assigning or granting something to a recipient.

zueinander.chain: A frozen adverb: ~zu~ ("to") + ~einander~ ("one another"), the latter itself ~ein~ + ~ander~, a reciprocal pronoun fused with its preposition and no longer inflected. The parallel with English ~to one another~ is exact, morpheme for morpheme; German simply writes it as one word and lets it behave as a separable particle.
senses: ~zueinander-~ marks reciprocity: the parties act toward each other.
The sense of ~zueinander-~ here is: of fitting, finding, or belonging — mutual suitability.

zufrieden.chain: A frozen prepositional phrase written as one word: ~zu~ + the old dative of ~Friede~ ("peace"), MHG ~ze vride~ ("in peace, content"). The noun goes back to Proto-Germanic *~friþuz~, from PIE *~preyH-~ ("to love, be dear"), the same root that gives English ~friend~ and ~free~. The modern one-word spelling hides a literal sense of being at peace.
senses: The sense of ~zufrieden~ here is: in a state of contentment, literally "at peace".
The sense of ~zufrieden~ here is the resultative frame: bring someone into that state (~zufriedenstellen~).
The sense of ~zufrieden~ here is: to settle for, to acquiesce in (~sich zufriedengeben~).

zugute.chain: A frozen prepositional phrase: ~zu~ + the old dative of the substantivized adjective ~gut~, MHG ~ze guote~ ("for the good, to the benefit"). It survives only in this fossilized adverbial shape, which is why it is written solid and why ~Gute~ here is no longer felt as a noun. The party benefited is the dative object of the verb.
senses: The sense of ~zugute-~ here is: to the benefit or advantage of someone.
The sense of ~zugute-~ here is: to accrue to, to be of use to (~zugutekommen~).
The sense of ~zugute-~ here is: to count something in someone's favor, to make allowance for it (~zugutehalten~).

zunichte.chain: A fossilized case form: ~zu~ + ~nichte~, the old dative of MHG ~niht~ ("nothing"), literally "to nothing". The dative ending is dead everywhere else in the modern language, so ~zunichte~ survives only in this phrase, chiefly ~zunichtemachen~ ("to bring to nothing, to destroy"). MHG ~niht~ is itself a contraction of ~ni~ + ~io~ + ~wiht~, "not ever a thing" — and that ~wiht~ is the same word as English ~wight~ and German ~Wicht~.
senses: ~zunichte-~ reduces something to nothing: destruction, annulment, frustration.
The sense of ~zunichte-~ here is: chiefly of hopes, plans, efforts, and agreements rather than physical objects.

zupass.chain: A frozen prepositional phrase: ~zu~ + ~Pass~ in its obsolete sense "fitting state, right measure". The noun is a Romance loan — MHG ~pas~ from Old French ~pas~, from Latin ~passus~ ("step, pace") — which acquired the figurative sense "suitability" under Middle Low German and Middle Dutch influence. By the sixteenth century ~zu paß~ meant "opportunely", and ~zupasskommen~ was built on it in the nineteenth, so this thoroughly German-looking particle is a cousin of English ~pace~, ~pass~, and ~passport~.
senses: ~zupass-~ marks timeliness: something arrives opportunely or suits the moment.
The sense of ~zupass-~ here is: used almost exclusively with ~kommen~.

zurecht.chain: A frozen prepositional phrase: MHG ~ze rehte~, the dative of ~reht~ ("right, what is proper") governed by ~ze~ ("to"). The phrase fused into a single adverb meaning "into proper order, rightly, as it should be," and the fusion is complete enough that modern speakers no longer hear the case ending inside it — ~zurechtlegen~ ("to lay out ready"), ~zurechtkommen~ ("to manage, get along"), ~zurechtweisen~ ("to reprimand"). ~Recht~ itself goes back to PIE *~h₃reǵ-~ ("to straighten, direct"), the root behind Latin ~rēctus~ and English ~right~.
senses: The sense of ~zurecht-~ here is: into proper order, into the right shape or arrangement.
The sense of ~zurecht-~ here is: correcting something that was wrong or out of place.
The sense of ~zurecht-~ here is: successfully, managing to cope with the circumstances.

zurück.chain: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). The first element goes back to PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"); the second to Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), whose further origin is uncertain. That second element is cognate with English ~ridge~ — a spine and a ridge are the same picture.
senses: The particle conveys return to a former place or state.
The particle conveys backward motion or retreat.
The particle conveys withdrawal — taking back what was given or said.

zusammen.chain: The adverb ~zusammen~, from MHG ~zesamene~, from OHG ~zisamane~ — ~zi~ ("to") plus ~samane~ ("together"), from Proto-Germanic *~samanē~, from PIE *~sem-~ ("one, together"). The second element is cognate with English ~same~ and, by way of Latin ~simul~ and ~similis~, with ~assemble~ and ~simultaneous~; Greek keeps it in ~homo-~.
senses: The particle conveys acting jointly, together with others.
The particle conveys combining separate things into one.
The particle conveys collapse — falling inward upon itself.

zuvor.chain: A frozen prepositional phrase: ~zu~ + ~vor~ ("before"), MHG ~ze vor~, an adverb of temporal priority meaning "beforehand, previously." As a particle it contributes the idea of getting there first. ~Zuvorkommen~ ("to forestall, to anticipate") yielded the adjective ~zuvorkommend~, which has drifted from "anticipating" to "obliging, courteous" — politeness reconceived as meeting a need before it is voiced.
senses: The sense of ~zuvor-~ here is: beforehand, previously, in advance.
The sense of ~zuvor-~ here is: getting there first, forestalling another (~zuvorkommen~).
The sense of ~zuvor-~ here is: doing something ahead of, or better than, someone else (~es jemandem zuvortun~).

zuwider.chain: A frozen phrase: ~zu~ + ~wider~ ("against"), literally "contrary to", governing the dative. It lives on as an adjective ("repugnant") and as a separable particle in the legal-register verbs ~zuwiderhandeln~ ("to contravene") and ~zuwiderlaufen~ ("to run counter to"). For the ~wider~ half — Proto-Germanic *~wiþrą~, cognate with English ~with~ in its old sense "against" — and for its confusability with ~wieder~ ("again"), see the ~wider~ entry.
senses: ~zuwider-~ marks contravention: acting against a rule, order, or law.
The sense of ~zuwider-~ here is: of an act or state running counter to something else.
The sense of ~zuwider-~ here is: chiefly legal and administrative register.

zwischen.chain: From the preposition ~zwischen~, MHG ~zwischen~, a reduction of OHG ~in zwiskēn~, the dative plural of ~zwiski~ ("twofold"), built on the numeral ~zwei~ ("two"). English ~between~ is built the very same way, from Old English ~be tweonum~ ("by twos"), so both languages arrived at "in the middle" by way of "among two." Cognate with Dutch ~tussen~ and with the ~twi-~ of English ~twilight~ and ~twin~.
senses: The sense of ~zwischen-~ here is: between two points, parties, or times.
The sense of ~zwischen-~ here is: interposed, inserted into an ongoing sequence (~zwischenlanden~, ~zwischenspeichern~).
The sense of ~zwischen-~ here is: provisional, done in the interval before the real thing.

ähnlich.chain: From the adjective ~ähnlich~ ("similar"), MHG ~anelīch~, from OHG ~analīh~, literally "of one form": ~ana~ ("on") + ~līh~ ("body, form"). That second element is the Proto-Germanic *~-līkaz~ that also produced English ~-ly~ and ~like~, so ~ähnlich~ and ~alike~ are formed on the same principle. Cognate with Dutch ~aanlijk~ (dialectal) and Old English ~anlīc~ ("alike").
senses: The sense of ~ähnlich~ here is: similar to, resembling.
The sense of ~ähnlich~ here is the resultative or perceptual frame: to look like someone (~ähnlichsehen~).

übel.chain: The adjective ~übel~ ("bad, ill, evil"), from MHG ~übel~, from OHG ~ubil~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubil~, from Proto-Germanic *~ubilaz~, probably from PIE *~upo-~ ("under, up from under"). Cognate with English ~evil~, Dutch ~euvel~, Gothic ~ubils~. Here it is adverbial rather than resultative: ~übelnehmen~ is to take a thing badly, hence to take offence, and ~übelwollen~ is to wish ill.
senses: The sense of ~übel~ here is: badly, ill — the manner in which the action is taken or meant.
The sense of ~übel~ here is in ~übelnehmen~: to take amiss, to hold against someone.
The sense of ~übel~ here is in ~übelwollen~: to bear ill will toward someone.

über.chain: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uber~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"), an extension of *~upo~ ("under, up from under"). Cognate with English ~over~, Dutch ~over~, Swedish ~över~, Latin ~super~, Ancient Greek ~hupér~, Sanskrit ~upári~.
senses: Stressed and separable, ~über-~ is literal and spatial: something moves over, across, or on top of something else.
It covers crossing to the other side — of a river, a street, a border.
With verbs of pouring or spilling it means "over the edge," of a container running over.
Unstressed and inseparable, the same particle takes abstract senses instead — excess, transfer, overlooking — and moves the verb's stress off the particle.

überein.chain: A fossilized prepositional phrase, MHG ~über ein~ ("into one, as one") — over into unity, that is, into agreement. It attached early to a small set of verbs, of which ~kommen~, ~stimmen~, and ~treffen~ survive; older German also had ~überein tragen~. The particle is no longer productive, and ~ein~ here is the numeral "one", not the particle ~ein-~ ("in, into").
senses: The sense of ~überein-~ here is: into agreement, into accord.
The sense of ~überein-~ here is: to one and the same result — matching, corresponding.
The sense of ~überein-~ here is no longer productive: bound to ~kommen~, ~stimmen~, ~treffen~.

übereinander.chain: The preposition ~über~ ("over") + the reciprocal pronoun ~einander~ ("one another"), itself ~ein~ + ~ander~ and the exact counterpart of English ~one another~. The whole means "one on top of the other," and it is transparently compositional; see the entry for ~über~. In ~übereinanderlegen~ and ~übereinanderschlagen~ it describes stacking or crossing, and in verbs of speech it means "about one another."
senses: ~übereinander-~ stacks or layers things one on top of another.
~übereinander-~ crosses one thing over another, as with legs or arms.
The sense of ~übereinander-~ here is: with verbs of speech, reciprocally about one another.

überhand.chain: A frozen noun phrase: MHG ~überhant~ ("superiority, the upper hand"), from ~über~ + ~Hand~, with ~überhant nemen~ attested from the 15th century. The metaphor is the one English preserves in ~gain the upper hand~ — the grasping hand stands for control. The fossilization is complete: ~Überhand~ survives in no construction other than ~überhandnehmen~, "to proliferate past all bounds".
senses: The sense of ~überhand-~ here is: the upper hand, mastery — a fossilized noun phrase.
The sense of ~überhand-~ here is in ~überhandnehmen~: to get out of hand, to proliferate, to become rampant.

übrig.chain: The adjective ~übrig~ ("remaining, left over"), from MHG ~überic~, ~überec~, formed with the suffix ~-ig~ on the preposition ~über~ ("over, above"), from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upér~ — the same root as English ~over~ and, through Greek and Latin, ~hyper-~ and ~super-~. The sense is what lies over and above the amount required.
senses: The sense of ~übrig~ here is: predicatively, "left over, remaining".
The sense of ~übrig~ here is: with ~lassen~, "to leave remaining".
The sense of ~übrig~ here is: with ~bleiben~, "to remain, to be all that is left".
